Recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have led to impressive performance in various applications, but their vulnerability to inaccurate label information and generated pseudo-labels is a pressing concern. Traditional pseudo-labeling methods have shown some success, but their limitations in maintaining consistency and preserving the underlying graph structure result in compounded errors and diminished accuracy. To address these issues, a novel approach called CALM is introduced, which enhances the pseudo-labeling process on GNNs through two main mechanisms. Firstly, CALM introduces a Calculus of Convergence module that regulates pseudo-labels to maintain consistency among similar nodes during the training process. Secondly, CALM incorporates a Calculus of Neighbors module that optimizes pseudo-labels by leveraging smoothness constraints among neighboring nodes with greater reliability. As a result, CALM produces higher-quality pseudo-labeled data and notable improvements in node classification accuracy, with experimental findings calibrating the accuracy of CALM at over 80% higher than baseline models.

This work introduces a novel neural network architecture called PatchNet, which is specifically designed for video object detection tasks. By leveraging spatial temporal separability in time, PatchNet streamlines computation, making it more efficient. The model outperforms a range of top-tier baseline architectures, including MobileNetV2, in both computational efficiency and accuracy. Notably, with a configuration of 8 sub-filters, we achieve state-of-the-art results on the DAVIS 2017 challenge, surpassing methods like SuperPoint+SuperMask while maintaining real-time processing capabilities.

The exclusion process on a one-dimensional lattice, known as totally asymmetric discrete time exclusion process (TASEP), is a well-known probabilistic model. Its study reveals varying distribution characteristics at different time points, heavily influenced by initial conditions, which can be complex to determine analytically for later time points. To overcome this challenge, researchers have applied machine learning techniques to investigate the effect of initial conditions on the multi-point distribution at distant distances in the system. Utilizing neural networks and data sets from simulations, researchers have successfully created a universal network that can accurately predict the distribution at distant times, based on the initial configuration of the system. This innovative approach, a first in its kind, provides new insights into the system's behavior at distant times and opens up the possibility of using machine learning to study other probabilistic models with complex initial conditions.

This study introduces a novel approach to enhancing the performance of wireless networks that integrate simultaneous information and energy transfer. We incorporate the Gaussian channel model into the distance-based information capacity formula to increase accuracy, then develop an optimized strategy that balances energy transfer and data transmission. This strategy involves adjusting antennas in the transmission and reception processes to achieve optimal results, influenced by the separation of antennas in both the receiving and transmitting devices. Results show that this strategy yields significant gains in energy transfer, up to 20 percent, compared to traditional methods, leading to improved energy efficiency and extended device battery life. Furthermore, our research highlights how to select the optimal level of antenna usage in the system.

We've developed a perturbation theory in SU(N) fermions that doesn't rely on specific group properties, resulting in second-order findings that are more complex than analogous U(N) and O(N) perturbation theory outcomes. Furthermore, our approach is flexible enough to be applied to a broader class of models, including SU(N) dimer models.

A widely used approach in quantum optomechanics involves modeling the interaction between light and mechanical objects using classical electromagnetic forces, which works particularly well for scenarios with high occupation numbers. This assumption has not been rigorously justified from a theoretical standpoint until now. By developing a Fock-state based treatment, we show that the phase-space based (classical) method is accurate only to first order in the mechanical occupation number n-bar, without relying on any specific initial state of the mechanical system. Notably, our research highlights significant discrepancies between the phase-space and Fock-state based methods when considering non-stationary states, such as squeezed states, indicating that squeeze-parameters must also be considered along with n-bar for an accurate representation.

The uniform asymptotic expansions for the orthogonal polynomials of generalised Freud weights are derived, which include the fictitious weight with a negative parameter for even n (referred to as the generalised Airy weight) and a sextic Freud weight for odd n. As a result, the latter can be considered an extension of the generalised Airy weight. Notably, the asymptotic expressions for the orthogonal polynomials hold true for all real values of the parameter a in the weight function. The explicit formulas for these polynomials are provided using either Chebyshev or Hermite polynomials. Furthermore, the uniform asymptotic formula for the coefficients of the monic orthogonal polynomials is also determined.

This research focuses on developing a distance sensor's effective field of view for a robotics application. By analyzing the distinct characteristics of each field, an optimal viewing area is identified for guiding a navigation robot's path. Initially, a distance field's entire 360-degree scope is mapped, and its boundaries are divided into horizontal segments, each representing a separate sub-field. These sub-fields are evaluated using two distance measurement methods to create a recognition algorithm that distinguishes adaptable from unresponsive fields. Lastly, simulation and real-world testing of a wall-following robot are carried out, comparing its trajectory when using only the main, refined field against the main, refined, and left sub-fields.

In the framework of perturbative algebraic quantum field theory, we investigate how to define subalgebras corresponding to localized, causal regions in a spacetime that has a boundary.  The test functions near the boundary are handled in two distinct ways: either by completely excluding them, or by limiting their support in a varying manner as it approaches the boundary.  The impact of these approaches on the theory, particularly with regard to regions away from the boundary, is examined.  When interpolation is applied, we demonstrate that certain test functions giving rise to distinct local theories can be identified, leading to differing interpretations of the equivalence relation for microlocal operators, and potentially resulting in nontrivial commutators between subalgebras associated with spacelike separated regions close to the boundary.

Smoke can significantly hinder visibility in surgical settings, posing a major safety concern. Smoke detection is essential for effective anesthetic administration, but current video-based detection methods struggle, particularly with low-quality footage. A novel, low-resource deep learning technique has been developed, utilizing a pre-trained model on the COCO dataset for initial feature extraction, rather than generating large amounts of smoke data for training. By utilizing a lightweight mobileNet architecture for the final classification of smoke and non-smoke images, this approach significantly reduces computational requirements. The model demonstrates high accuracy, reaching 98.5% in detecting smoke from low-resolution footage.

Molmer-Sorensen gates are a crucial tool for creating high-fidelity connections between qubits, and variations of these gates have been developed to better cope with the effects of fluctuating magnetic fields. By designing a model that takes into consideration interactions between multiple ions, researchers discovered a hidden influence that reduces the rate at which connections form, and under specific conditions, formed connections can even reverse direction. The conditions under which these variations perform optimally were identified, and simulations showed that they can be resistant to fluctuations to within a very high degree. The impact of imperfections on their overall accuracy was also examined, and it's suggested that experiments should aim to minimize the influence of certain high-frequency fluctuations that affect how these gates function.

Using advanced ab-initio computations, researchers investigated how equilibrium conditions affect cation positioning in three perovskite compounds: BaTiO$_3$, NaTaO$_3$, and NaBiO$_3$. By calculating the energy barriers for atomic displacement, they found that reducing the equilibrium volume significantly increases off-centering in all compounds. Notably, substituting larger barium ions with sodium ions significantly increases displacement for both titanium and sodium ions. In contrast, sodium ions display significantly lower displacement levels compared to their equivalent larger cations. These findings suggest that the theoretical predictions of phase transitions based on atomic off-centering may be more reliable when using materials like NaBiO$_3$, which exhibits a theoretical Curie temperature (Tc) close to 200K.

In recent years, there has been a significant push in research towards developing dynamic models that can adapt to changing concepts in time-series data within machine learning. This adaptation often involves making strong, individually defined assumptions that can be inefficient to implement on large datasets. This work introduces multivariate Gaussian processes as a flexible framework for representing time-series that are conditionally independent of each other in a graphical model sense. The study delves into creational and destructive transformations of undirected graphs to parameterize complex processes that can be trained efficiently using conjugate properties. A novel machine learning method is proposed to learn the graph's structure by maximizing the performance of the process it represents. This approach is demonstrated through time-series analysis on simulated and real-world data that undergo changes in dynamics, showing the potential of learned processes to effectively track shifts in underlying models over time.

We developed and studied a method for applying the full configuration interaction (FCI) approach to accurate ground state calculations that utilizes recurrent quantum circuit patterns for efficient computation of ground state wave function properties. These circuit patterns, consisting of alternating layers of unitary coupled cluster transformations and variable encodings, were shown in theoretical analysis and practical quantum simulations on a noisy quantum processor to significantly reduce resource requirements. Specifically, our recurrent structure was found to allow for a linear scaling improvement in both gate and depth resources, while maintaining high fidelity for FCI state transformations even with increased measurement depths.

We introduce the Generalized Chebyshev method, a family of optimization algorithms that integrate insights from the optimal convergence rate of Chebyshev's template algorithm and successful strategies in nonconvex optimization. This new class of methods surpasses the performance of widely used algorithms, such as gradient descent, in average-case performance for smooth functions, and we provide explicit formulas for the parameters that yield superior results. Furthermore, the algorithm can be adapted to function value minimization and zero-finding problems across various problem types, including smooth functions, polynomial systems, and min-eigvalue problems.

Moiré superlattices exhibit unique properties due to their large energy scales, low energy excitations, and strong coupling. Recent experiments have shown that twisted bilayer graphene and other moiré systems can host low-energy excitations influenced by interlayer excitons, which can be controlled by an electric field. However, calculating the effects of interlayer excitons in moiré systems is computationally challenging, limiting theoretical insights. In this study, we develop a theoretical framework using a quantum field theory approach to model the thermodynamic properties of interlayer excitons in moiré systems. By doing so, we can systematically calculate low-energy responses and their dependence on interaction strength. Our approach is validated by comparing it to known results for simpler systems, and applying the framework to predict behavior in twisted bilayer graphene, we find that excitation of interlayer excitons leads to a distinct energy scale, separate from the band gap, that persists at higher temperatures where single-particle excitations are thermally suppressed.

This research focuses on developing an efficient method for accurately locating a moving object under uncertain and changing environments. An advanced probabilistic data association method is proposed, capable of handling multiple targets, high frame rates, and dynamic lighting conditions. By incorporating an adaptive weight system that adjusts processing complexity based on available resources, this method optimally utilizes system capabilities. Furthermore, a dynamic neighbor identification system is implemented to restrict calculations to nearby targets, enhancing the algorithm's responsiveness in real-time applications. Extensive testing validates the method's ability to adjust to varying levels of system load and lighting conditions, and its superior performance over current techniques in similar tasks.

The ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has analyzed data collected with a data-taking rate of 140 TeV$^{-1}$ from TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ of TeV$^{-1}$ of TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$ at TeV$^{-1}$

We establish a one-to-one correspondence between transverse, traceless gravitational modes, in the form of spin-2 fields, and soft theorems, using examples from conformal gravity, general relativity, and anti-de Sitter space. By applying this connection, we identify the vacuum state, vacuum transitions, and interaction processes. Specifically, this relationship shows that the vacuum corresponds to a state where the Cotton tensor is zero, consistent with the expectation from spin-3 current conservation. Furthermore, the requirement that the spin-2 field is a conserved gauge current results in the fully nonlinear equations of motion described by the Einstein Hilbert action.

A comprehensive investigation into a comprehensive ordering of compact, zero-dimensional, infinite topological spaces has been conducted. This ordering has specific properties and we have determined which compact spaces are equivalent under this ordering by establishing a equivalence relationship. This equivalence leads to a method for constructing a comprehensive orthomodular lattice from each compact ordered space. We then demonstrate how to create an orthomodular space whose underlying set of points corresponds to the construction of the lattice, preserving the compactness and topological structure. This allows us to create a compact model for any given compact ordered space as part of the equivalence classification.

The exponential increase in the amount of digital content has led to a significant problem, namely the overwhelming amount of information that needs to be managed, making it difficult for individuals to find relevant information. In order to address this challenge, text generation techniques have been applied across various domains, enabling more efficient access to and utilization of unstructured data. In order to facilitate further analysis, the text that is generated must also allow users to provide valuable feedback. In order to achieve this goal, this research proposes a neural network-based approach that can automatically create visual representations of proofs, thereby enabling users to annotate and revise the generated content. The generated visual representations can be further utilized to break down the proof into more manageable sections, making it easier for users to locate and address specific errors during the review process. A fundamental component of the proposed system is an encoder-decoder neural network architecture, combined with a sequence-to-sequence model that can learn the structure of the encoded proof. This system was evaluated through a series of experiments that demonstrated its effectiveness in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

We will leverage modifications of Watson's formula, along with advancements made by Soundararajan and Harper, to calculate higher-order moments of $L$-functions. The performance of our approach will be compared with the method used by Soundararajan in his analysis of the second moment of the Riemann zeta function, particularly for increasing thresholds. The framework presented here can also be applied to investigate the behavior of centred moments within a family of $L$-functions.

Interior point methods remain one of the most reliable approaches for resolving intricate optimization challenges across a variety of domains, such as power systems and the planning of networks. Initial proposals suggested performing interiors with varying levels of precision, but current implementations typically follow a one-size-fits-all model, only adjusting step sizes to maintain precision. We suggest an innovative interior point framework that tailors the complexity of inner loop iterations to their respective degrees of precision requirements, and one that can be applied to various types of linear and quadratic equations, such as those found in the planning of DC AC systems and the optimization of costs. By making this adaptive interior method one that is more efficient, it now offers the capacity to terminate inner iterations at an earlier stage, thus making it faster on average. We have tested this method on a range of problems, such as those involving the planning of DC AC systems, and the results show an improvement of up to 40% in performance, compared to the traditional interior point methods, as validated against a number of optimization problems, such as those found in the research on network planning.

The A_gq^(3)(N) transition is essential in the variable flavor number scheme to incorporate heavy quarks into perturbative QCD calculations at the third order. By examining how three-parton operators in heavy-quark flavor schemes relate to those in schemes lacking heavy-quarks, we can determine the A_gq^(3)(N) formules for N=2, 3, 4. These calculations confirm previously obtained A_gq^(3)(N) formules and show they're consistent with those derived using heavy-quark coefficient functions, specifically c_q^(3)(N). Furthermore, we find that the sum of A_gq^(3)(N) and relevant terms in A_qq^(3)(N) and A_qg^(3)(N) matches the sum of their heavy-quark counterparts, thereby verifying a previously proposed flavor number scheme sum rule.

AI incidents encompass a broad range of events, including flaws, accidents, and successes, associated with AI systems. AI Incident Database (AIED) is a freely accessible, online repository that catalogs incidents related to AI systems, allowing contributors to submit, edit, and delete entries, as well as retrieve relevant information. The database serves two primary purposes: it provides a comprehensive overview of incidents in AI-powered intelligent systems to facilitate learning from experiences and shares specific case studies to inform the AI community. The site is easily navigable and features incident descriptions, as well as a detailed Wiki that explains the categorization framework and various analytical reports generated from the contributed data.

Employing the functional approach to renormalization, specifically using functional differential equations, we identify a refined method for renormalizing large-N Yang-Mills theory. By applying this strategy, we derive an exact functional differential equation for the effective average action, known as the ERG equation, which, when analyzed in a specific approximation, allows us to refine the Ward identities' structure, thereby ensuring the renormalizability of the system, gateway to demonstrating the asymptotic freedom of pure Yang-Mills theory.

In cloud environments, multiple processes can interact, creating challenges for owners who need to ensure that their processes adhere to specifications, particularly when there are contradictions among those specifications. A monitoring system in cloud settings can handle specification conflicts in real-time by generating dynamic requirements on-the-fly, allowing for instant detection of operational deviations. A model-based monitoring approach is presented in this paper, based on the MDD2OAL framework, which supports the development of procedural and interactive models, with one model type representing the cloud system to be monitored and the other acting as a dynamic, online monitor. Together, these models form an interactive system, with the framework automatically generating the monitor's code in a targeted language, such as JavaScript, for online deployment in the cloud system's execution environment, enabling real-time requirement verification and deviation reporting within the specified execution context. To demonstrate the approach's capabilities, a case study on verifying requirements in cloud deployments is provided, along with performance evaluations of model-based and traditional monitoring methods.

This text presents a formal system, Proto-Quipper-M, built upon a logical foundation to specify and test quantum circuits reliably, all within a computable framework. By integrating key quantum principles like the unclonable nature of quantum states and the probabilistic outcomes of measurements, the system accurately reflects the limitations inherent in quantum mechanics. A nuanced distinction between constructible and unconstructible states, coupled with a logical structure, enables the expression of quantum rules, while an associated computational model ensures the rules are enforceable in actual quantum circuits. The computation model, computed through Monte-Carlo simulation, verifies expressions containing logical constructs within the system.

We've applied a fundamental concept, finite-size scaling, to a broad class of random-matrix models with eigenvalues constrained to the lower half of a complex plane, encompassing the Laguerre, Wigner-Dyson-Mehta, and Marchenko-Pastur ensembles. By utilizing the Gibbs measure, measure-density, and scaling-hypothesis relations, our framework enables the derivation of unique mathematical properties that connect individual behavior of restricted-matrix ensembles to their theoretical counterparts, effectively removing large-N approximations. This approach also provides opportunities to make numerical validations and offers potential applications such as modeling singular-value distributions from random matrices with structured disorder, which may have implications for fields like signal processing, geostatistics, and cosmology.

We explore the use of two-mode squeezing for enhancing the detection of an optical phase using a continuous optical system. The system, consisting of a radiation pressure loop, involves beam splitters and mirrors on a optical path, with squeezed light and optical carriers as key components. Our research demonstrates that two-mode squeezing can boost the performance of quantum-enhanced phase sensing in this particular setup.

As genomic sequencing technology advances and produces more detailed data, there is a growing need for efficient tools to process and analyze the overwhelming amounts of information generated. One such tool, multiway number partitioning, has been shown to effectively accelerate genome assembly, a critical process in genetics research. This paper presents a novel algorithm, Tree Balancing Algorithm (TBA), which utilizes a dynamically adjusted binary tree to evenly distribute overlapping ranges across multiple processors, thereby optimally balancing computational load. Load, a key metric in computer science, measures the disparity in processing time between the fastest and slowest processors, and lower is better. Through extensive testing on over 50,000 datasets using simulated and real-overlapping ranges, TBA's superiority over existing methods is confirmed, showcasing significant improvements in lower load values.

The paper introduces a modified logistic logistic equation with a delay, which is formulated as $\dot{u}(t) = -\alpha \tanh\left(\beta \int_{t-\tau}^{t} u(s) \, ds\right)$ for real-valued functions $u$ in the $L^\infty_{\tau}(\mathbb{R}^+, \mathbb{R})$ space, where the parameters $\alpha, \beta, \tau$ are positive real numbers. This modified model guarantees the convergence of any solution to a stable, positive equilibrium. In the context of a cell population model with a time-dependent harvesting rate $\tau(t)$, where the rate is defined as $\tau(t) = \int_{t-\tau(t)}^{t} u(s) \, ds$, various cases of the rate's behavior - including being a step function or following a power law - are examined. Additionally, several theorems on the continuity of solutions with respect to the delay parameter are presented, along with an asymptotic analysis of the delay parameter's influence on the solutions.

The Isometric Log-Ratio (ILR) transformation has found widespread application in various fields, such as ecology, geology, and bioinformatics, to analyze compositional data. However, the 'constancy of scale' benefit of the ILR transformation has yet to be applied to the analysis of data comprising event sequences, known as point processes. Some previous research has attempted to analyze the composition of event sequences using specific metrics, such as inter-arrival times, AIC, or log-likelihood ratios, but these methods cannot be directly applied to compositions that evolve over time. Building on previous work in counting process regression, this work extends the transformation to point processes by defining a general composition of counting processes and demonstrating that the Isometric Log-Ratio (ILR) space offers advantages in terms of constancy of scale, thus enabling direct regression of composed inter-arrival times while preserving geometric structures, all within a Karlin-McCulloh martingale framework. A simulation study is conducted to evaluate the proposed model and compare it to traditional regression methods that rely on a specific parametric assumption, namely the Cox process, highlighting the proposed method's flexibility in accommodating various types of processes without strict parametric assumptions.

Research on quantum circuits of increasing complexity has led researchers to explore large-scale hybrid quantum systems capable of amplifying and entangling quantum states. Researchers have developed the technology to create and manipulate entangled Cooper pairs in mesoscopic quantum devices, allowing them to study their fundamental quantum behavior. This special issue of Nature Physics will explore the latest advancements in this field, focusing on the underlying principles of quantum phenomena in devices that incorporate superconductors and provide the platform for quantum information processing and potentially, fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Investigations into the collective properties of deformed nuclei, particularly the softness of the gamma and beta shapes, have been conducted within the framework of the energy-based macroscopic-microscopic model. By analyzing quadrupole and hexadecupole moments, as well as energy levels and collective wave functions of the lowest quadrupole and hexadecupole states in even-even nuclei from nickel to samarium, specific trends in nuclear shape transitions have been identified. A notable shift from spherical to ellipsoidal or triangular nuclear shapes is observed at neutron number 40 in both nickel and germanium, yet nickel exhibits a sudden shift to a more spherical configuration at neutron number 50, in contrast to germanium, which displays a smooth transition. Near neutron number 50, nuclei exhibiting a significant prolate shape include isotopes with 48, 49, and 410, as well as the pseudomagic nucleus of lead-208, which exhibits an oblate shape.

A beam and storage ring intersection technique has been used to measure light, neutron-deficient isotopes with short half-lives. New experimental results for 102Te, 102Sb, 101Sb, and 101Sn have been presented. The Te$^{2+}$, Sb$^{3+}$, and Sn$2+$ ions were produced via a 102Sn beam and separated by a high-resolution magnetic separator, with measurements of the 102Te to 102Sb and 101Sn to 101Sb beta-decay half-lives yielding 21(4) s and 13(2) s, respectively. Additionally, 101Sn$^{2+}$ ions were allowed to decay to 101In and measurements of the 101Sn to 101In beta-decay half-life gave a value of 3.3(3) s. The 102Sn$^{2+}$ beam was also allowed to decay in flight, with a measurement of the 102Sn to 102Sb beta-decay half-life of 30.3(3) s.

Machine learning models that adapt to specific tasks are developing rapidly in various fields, yet they struggle to comply with fundamental physical principles. By integrating principles from quantum field theory, we can build NCFlow, a U(1) gauge-invariant framework for quantum electrodynamics. Our approach involves introducing electron and photon fields within a electron-positron annihilation and hadron collider dataset. Utilizing the Fermi-Dirac and Planck distributions, we derive the initial fields. For hadron collider data, initial electron and photon fields are also derived from the corresponding distributions. The electron and photon fields are then embedded into the electron-positron and hadron collider datasets. The NCFlow model is trained using the embedded datasets and the loss function that minimizes the difference between the dataset distribution and the prior distribution. Our results show that the NCFlow model is capable of accurately modeling the electron-positron and hadron collider datasets while maintaining the principles of QED.

This research focuses on the effectiveness of utilizing biased sampling to increase text-to-text generation accuracy, specifically in tasks where the target text adheres to a predefined template, such as in document understanding. By employing biased sampling during the decoding phase, we achieve significant improvements of up to 20 percentage points in biasing-based models and up to 10 percentage points in non-biased models. Moreover, experiments demonstrate that utilizing biased sampling not only allows models to perform on par with superior models designed for specific tasks, but also retains bias-free outputs. Furthermore, biased sampling exhibits robustness against adversarial attacks.

Our analysis covers top quark production at an integrated luminosity of 37 nanobarns, recorded by the CMS experiment at LHC 8 TeV, resulting in a cross-section of 157.3 nanobarns, consistent with QCD predictions, with an associated uncertainty of 5.2 nanobarns, accounting for systematic considerations.

This paper introduces a novel quantum framework that guarantees accurate outcomes even when database information is unavailable. To achieve this, we incorporate two methods: one uses measurement results to adjust parameters and optimize execution outcomes, and the other employs Grover's database search algorithm to adjust database information. A search algorithm is also developed to adjust both the database and optimization parameters, ensuring execution accuracy. This research is an exploration of quantum arithmetic operations and does not introduce a new algorithmic approach to execution.

We conducted a detailed analysis of the angular clustering of galaxies from the Low Frequency Array Low-sky Test, which is an deep radio survey covering 3.5 square degrees of the sky toward the North Celestial Pole. Focusing on galaxies between 0.3 and 1.5 GHz with source counts exceeding 0.5 sources per square degree, we derived the two-point correlation function for each sample and broke it down into components based on the source count density. By combining these components, we obtained the total angular clustering statistic for each LoTSS sample. Comparing our results with $\Lambda$CDM predictions using the code AngularPower, which incorporates the latest measurements of the Hubble constant and the angular diameter distance to the last scattering surface from the Planck mission, we found good agreement across all LoTSS galaxy samples. This good match indicates that our method of adding components based on source counts accurately represents the angular clustering of galaxies. With the LoTARR path-NP dataset expected to provide source counts one order of magnitude brighter than the current LoTSS samples while maintaining the same angular resolution, we anticipate that the method of decomposing the angular clustering into components will enable precise constraints on $\Lambda$CDM cosmology parameters when the data becomes available.

The Lasso technique effectively regularizes linear models and helps prevent overfitting. Researchers have expanded its scope to a rank-constrained context, resulting in the Lasso problem for high-dimensional data matrices. Due to its computational infeasibility, researchers proposed the "approximate Lasso" as an approximation, which further deviates from the original problem. "Rank Lasso" was then introduced as a more accurate approximation, which we approximate using an alternative model derived from a modified linear system. By applying an innovative approach known as "adaptive sieving," we efficiently solve large matrices, taking advantage of sparsity and the low-rank structure of our algorithm. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our method produces results comparable to "approximate Lasso" while being significantly faster and achieving a precise solution to the original rank-lasso problem.

We demonstrate in this study that in quantum thermodynamics, there is a singular, universal optimal protocol for achieving the maximum entropy production in a two-level system initially in a thermal state coupled to a dynamic bath. This finding stands in contrast to previous work where the maximum entropy production rate was found to be attainable through multiple distinct optimal protocols. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this result on the proposed quantum generalization of the Fl\'{e}ry theorem.

To effectively address climate change, various initiatives are leveraging the computational capabilities of AI, yet the carbon footprint of AI itself poses a concern. In response, a concept called ecoAI has been proposed to explore AI as a means to assess the environmental impact of other AI services. By analyzing training data, model designs, and algorithm performance, ecoAI is envisioned to provide comprehensive metrics, such as memory usage, energy consumption, and latency, for AI services. In turn, these metrics will enable building and testing virtual systems, ultimately leading to more energy-efficient AI deployment through optimized containerization. This paper presents the foundational work towards ecoAI, outlining its proposed framework, initial findings, and potential benefits.

Prescriptive process monitoring method development often relies on simulated data due to the unavailability of labeling information from UNP/M data. However, to ensure the methods are effective in real-world data analysis, their performance in artificial environments must reflect their performance in actual data. This study introduces an approach to validate and fine-tune VM development using a combination of backtesting and machine learning techniques applied to planning data from a manufacturing company. The proposed method treats VM development as a classification problem and employs performance metrics that are independent of specific thresholds. The results demonstrate that the validation process successfully identifies and addresses issues in the originally developed rules, leading to notable enhancements in their performance both in terms of areas under the ROC curve and the accuracy rate.

A method to estimate the error in a coupled problem, based on a dual-weighted residual approach, is introduced and tested on solving the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations using a cell-based discontinuous Galerkin method. This dual-weighted residual method utilizes an auxiliary approach to ensure that the residual is properly constrained by a compatible function space. Several alternative methods for imposing constraints are discussed, with a particular focus on a large eddy simulation of a cylinder's flow, demonstrating that a locally refined approach effectively captures the coupled Lagrange multiplier equations, pressure, and velocity fields at a low cost.

Graph packing problems, particularly those involving vertex-disjoint paths or cycles, are notoriously difficult to bound tightly due to the lack of clear theoretical limitations. Although path packing algorithms have strong practical performance, their results are only guaranteed to be within a factor of three of the optimal integer solution from a long time ago, a bound that dates back to 1979. This study presents a significant improvement on this factor, demonstrating that the maximum set of vertex-disjoint paths in a graph can at most be $(1.5+\epsilon)$ times larger than the output of a path packing algorithm for any given small positive value of $\epsilon$. This bound applies not only to unweighted graphs, but also to directed graphs when finding the longest path set.

This study explores the dynamics of one-dimensional opinions influenced by random and weak interactions. A key aspect of our research involves demonstrating how the system's clique formation arises naturally from the dynamics, rather than being imposed. Furthermore, our findings show that the clique sizes are governed by these interaction parameters. By leveraging theoretical insights gained from a model based on continuous opinions, we gained a deeper understanding of the underlying physics of clique formation. Moreover, our results reveal how the system's clique evolution follows a universal and sub-exponential pattern.

Our research delves into the study of an asymptotically flat electrostatic scalar hair ball mode, a phenomenon previously identified when employing complex scalars. We demonstrate that it's feasible to generalize this mode to include complex potentials, with the understanding that it has significant implications for holographic superconductors. Moreover, our findings reveal that it's possible to create stable, hair-covered black holes through controlled gradual introduction of scalar hair, with implications extending to the realm of holographic superconductors.

Our model provides a theoretical explanation for the observed correlation between gene length and the time lag between transcription and mature mRNA availability, known as nascent mRNA accumulation. We establish a diffusion-based mechanism for this relationship, which is supported by our analytical proof. Moreover, our model aligns with the body of existing empirical evidence and offers a framework for further investigation into underlying gene expression processes and dynamics.

Scanning the table of isotopes in the region 58Ni along the neutron number with increased Ni isotopes, we examine the behavior of the N = 40 subshell gap, which is associated with the monopole interaction, using experimental and theoretical data. Focusing on 64Ni, we investigate particle excitations using the 64Ni(p,d) 63Ni and 64Ni(d,p) 63Ni reactions, which involve the removal or addition of a neutron, respectively. Employing the shell model, we calculate the energy levels up to 10 MeV, using the F0, G0, and C10 neutron and proton interactions, which reveal that high-energy states are dominated by different configurations. Notably, we find that despite data suggesting the N = 40 gap decreases in Ni isotopes, 63Ni exhibits a subshell gap behavior distinct from other isotopes, with certain high-energy states being weakly excited in 63Ni, indicating a significant energy gap. Furthermore, we find that particle interactions using both types of reactions yield consistent results, supporting the concept of a shell model with a variable interaction, and with data suggesting the N = 40 gap is smaller in 63Ni, we propose that the shell gap is approximately 5 MeV, indicating a substantial energy gap.

The Weyl fermions in the Adjoint representation impact SU(N) gauge theories' dynamics, and our study, utilizing large-N perturbation theory, examines the effects of Weyl fermions on the SU(N) gauge coupling's beta function, particularly for N=2 and N>=3. The analysis reveals an anomaly of 2/N in the beta function, and this effect diminishes with increasing N. By integrating this anomaly into the theory of Weyl fermions, our consideration expands upon prior research, and our findings are consistent with proposed constraints on the beta function, and we discuss the implications for conformal theories based on Weyl fermions, and large-N coupling constants.

A new type of code, known as a group code, has been developed using an abelian finite group, combining matrix theory and the concept of circulant codes. We establish the relationship between a group code and its associated ideal, then derive the parameters of the code, its weight distribution, and the properties of its dual, including the properties of its transpose. We demonstrate that the code is self-dual or equivalent to its dual transpose under certain conditions. We also present the matrix structure of the code and prove its equivalence to a specific block circulant code, which may lead to efficient constructions. Additionally, we propose two methods for constructing group codes, resulting in a list of newly created codes. We also examine the parameters of the code when the group order is square-free, and establish the parameters for the code when using specific fields and prime numbers. We calculate the minimum distance bound and identify the parameters for the code when using specific fields and prime numbers, including the case when the field is a quadratic extension of a prime field. We generate some new maximum-rank-metric self-dual polar codes.

Our work is centered around an advanced algorithm, Bucket Elimination, a highly efficient variant of the message passing approach for reasoning about complex models. By leveraging this algorithm, we have developed a suite of sophisticated tools, including methods for optimizing and analyzing mathematical calculations as well as structural simplifications, all of which are accelerated through parallel computation techniques, such as GPU utilization and task scheduling on multiple CPU cores, leading to substantial performance boosts of up to two orders of magnitude.

Our proposed approach to detecting and localizing fallen items from video footage leverages both the visual data and audio cues, incorporating fundamental physical principles to guide the item identification process. This is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving transparent surfaces, such as glass tables, where visual information alone might not suffice. By linking audio signals with the laws of acoustics, our system can accurately locate and identify the fallen objects, even in real-time. This approach has proven effective in localizing and identifying multiple objects, with high accuracy rates of up to 94% for short videos, allowing us to even identify smaller and lighter objects, such as coins and buttons, that might be challenging to detect using acoustics alone.

Continuing our investigation into the universality of jamming transitions, we now examine systems with a uniform and frictionless transition as well as a frictional shear transition. We achieve this by applying various types of shear to compact groups of isotropic and frictional particles. Our decision to study the isotropic and shear universality classes for both frictionless and frictional systems is based on the presence of these characteristics rather than their respective modes. We found that the critical exponents for frictionless isotropic and frictionless shear jamming transitions are distinct, whereas a self-duality relationship exists such that the critical exponents for both shear and isotropic jamming transitions among frictional particles are identical.

This paper introduces the MS($k$)-AR($p$) family, an extension of traditional AR($p$) models, designed to model time series influenced by unobserved, shifting states. We focus on electricity demand and show that an MS($2$)-AR($4$) model outperforms standard autoregressive models in capturing dynamics, surpassing their exogenous factor-driven versions. An effective estimation method for this family is developed using a novel, simplified optimization technique. We leverage public electricity demand data from the European Union to validate our approach, confirming its superiority over conventional methods.

We conducted a comprehensive study to examine the level of awareness among various public sector professionals regarding algorithmic biases in Web search results. This research involved conducting 12 in-depth interviews to gain a better understanding of how these professionals perceive and utilize search engines in their daily work, as well as their awareness of potential biases influencing search outcomes. Although interviewees acknowledged using search engines to inform their decisions, they generally dismissed the notion of inherent biases in search results, often attributing any perceived disparities to differences in information availability rather than skewed search results. While some professionals recognized the value of diverse perspectives, they expressed skepticism about the effectiveness of search engines in providing such diversity, particularly when searching for information related to marginalized communities. To effectively address this concern, interviewees recommended incorporating various credibility indicators into search results, including both system-generated and user-driven metrics.

Our proposed system, Synthesis Framework, is designed to create programs by synthesizing their components within a hierarchical structure, allowing for the application of domain-specific programs to synthesize simpler ones within an ordered tree format. The framework operates successfully in multiple settings, including synthesizing 2D shape transformation pipelines, generating image editing pipelines, and creating video generation workflows on platforms such as RunwayML and Adobe Premiere Pro. Despite the vast search space potential, our framework efficiently handles large instances, effectively producing syntheses for 126 applications within minutes, often within around 2 minutes on average. The framework operates by first constructing a hierarchical structure of applicable domain-specific programs based on their output compatibility, then uses a method to effectively populate this structure with random programs or specific goals. The framework also demonstrates the versatility of our approach in synthesizing complex tasks like video generation workflows, achieving an average synthesis time of around 2 minutes. The source code for our system is publicly available on GitHub.

Climate change is a pressing global issue, and to address it, scientists employ complex computer models of the Earth's atmosphere. However, these models are extremely complex and have an overwhelming number of parameters, making them difficult to use. Researchers have developed methods to reduce the number of parameters while maintaining accurate predictions, but these methods are limited by the need to pre-select which parameters to reduce. This pre-selection process, which is often based on expert knowledge, can be biased and may not reflect the full range of interactions between the parameters. A new approach, which is inspired by quantum physics, allows the parameters to be in a'superposition' of different states until a measurement is made. This new approach, when combined with computer simulations, provides a more accurate representation of the parameters and their interactions, leading to better results in the parameter reduction process.

Gravitational wave detectors anticipate that fine structure lines in the infrared, specifically those at wavelengths of 75, 108, and under certain conditions up to 120 micrometers, can be utilized as indicators of kilonovae. The James Webb Space Telescope's Mid-Infrared Facility is ideally suited for detecting the stronger spectral lines at 75 and 108 micrometers, with a sensitivity potentially good enough to be triggered by a kilonova within days following a gravitational wave event. The Gravitational Wave Optical Universe Finder's near-infrared capabilities allow for broader searches in the optical spectrum, enabling follow-up studies up to hundreds of megaparsecs away. The synergy between these two space telescopes could revolutionize our understanding of these phenomena, making them the most effective detectors for fine structure lines in the future.

X-ray beam delivery in radiation oncology is hindered by real-time obstacles such as moving organs and tumors, requiring constant adjustments to maintain accurate and effective delivery. The challenges extend beyond this, encompassing safe delivery away from adjacent sensitive areas and ensuring precise delivery for fast-moving targets. Recent advancements in technology, specifically fast electron linear accelerators and intelligent control systems, present promising solutions to mitigate these challenges. We outline the requirements for next-generation beam delivery systems, highlighting the need for real-time feedback control and efficient communication between systems to adapt to dynamic treatment conditions. A novel framework is proposed, featuring an advanced X-ray beam tracking system, designed to monitor and respond to moving obstacles in real-time, ensuring safe and precise delivery of treatment.

In the analysis of high-dimensional compositional data, log-transformed components are commonly used to transform a compound distribution into an approximate normal distribution N_p(μ, I). However, traditional estimation techniques like maximum likelihood estimation often struggle to provide accurate results in the analysis of such complex data sets. This paper presents a novel estimation method for multivariate Laplace distribution Lap_p(0, I), known as the Composite Multivariate Laplace Distribution (CMLD), which is the convolution of independent Laplace distributions, along with statistical tests to determine whether two CMLDs are similar. Furthermore, this research introduces two methods to estimate the CMLD's parameters and tests whether two CMLDs are similar, ultimately developing a maximum likelihood estimator for the CMLD and a generalized likelihood ratio test to compare two CMLDs, which can be applied in statistical comparisons between groups, such as in the analysis of microbiome data.

Recent discoveries of numerous exoplanets have provided scientists with an opportunity to validate or refute prevailing theories of planet formation. Although the core accretion model successfully accounts for the high abundance of terrestrial planets, it poses a challenge in explaining the distinct distribution of gas giant planets, particularly the likelihood of runaway gas accretion. To bridge this discrepancy, researchers have proposed the idea that gas giant formation is facilitated by the availability of solid material in the protoplanetary disk. Utilizing advanced statistical methods, this research analyzes a vast dataset of exoplanets to assess the frequency and properties of solid material available for planet formation. By applying these techniques, findings reveal that the overall likelihood of gas giant creation is on par with the predictions of the core accretion model, yet the fitter parameters indicate that the process of runaway gas accretion may be facilitated by the presence of solid material. Ultimately, these results imply that the majority of gas giant planets are likely to undergo re-accretion or fall apart due to the dynamic processes of planetary systems evolving over time.

Intelligence is closely tied to an individual's capacity to learn from incomplete information, requiring the tracking of hidden states that are not directly observable. A key component of this capability is a memory system that can be enhanced by a Kaspian, an advanced software agent operating within a simulated robot environment. By leveraging internal memory structures, Kaspian is able to generate accurate forecasts, even when its perceptions are limited. Our analysis of Kaspian's decision-making processes within a complex navigation task reveals the significance of memory management in intelligent behavior.

We examine indirect detection opportunities for a dark matter model, known as the Higgs-portal model, in which a dark matter particle interacts with the SM Higgs. Our analysis focuses on the impact of the scalar mediator's mass on the dark matter's detectability, considering masses lighter or heavier than half of the dark matter particle's mass. For mediator masses significantly lighter than the dark matter particle, we observe that production and detection cross sections remain relatively constant across a broad range of energies, making dark matter detectable across multiple channels. Conversely, for mediator masses heavier than half of the dark matter particle, production and detection are concentrated around specific energies corresponding to the mediator mass, making dark matter more vulnerable to detection at a particular energy threshold. Our comparison of the model with recent observations from the Fermi-LAT for gamma-rays and the Higgs LHC searches reveals model constraints that vary based on the mediator's mass, with the model falling below predicted astrophysical gamma-ray limits for both light and heavy mediator masses. Furthermore, we find that for heavy mediator masses, future collisions at the LHC will provide more comprehensive constraints on the dark matter parameter space.

A novel, comprehensive, and scalable collection of cognitive tasks, the Mod-Cog battery, builds upon existing sets like CogState and n-back by offering greater task diversity, simplicity, and complexity while allowing for easy extension and customisation of the cognitive domain.

We investigate the geometric structure of nilpotent algebra varieties, focusing on 
their properties in terms of algebraic completeness, dimension, and homogeneity. 
Using a combinatorial framework, we establish a method for classifying families of 
polynomial representations of varieties up to equivalence. Through this classification, 
distinct families within each variety type are identified and catalogued. 
This systematic approach enables the dimensonal measurement of each nilpotent algebra 
variety, resulting in a comprehensive list of possible dimensions for each type. 
Additionally, examples from lower dimensions illustrate the diversity and complexity 
of these geometric structures.

The most prominent feature of radiating plasma in relativistic jets is the dominant role played by high-speed electrons in the plasma. The intense radiation emitted by these electrons, combined with their high density and speed, can lead to significant energy transfer from Cosmic Microwave Background photons to the electrons through the inverse Compton process. The resulting energy exchange can drive plasma dynamics and influence the plasma's behavior. The purpose of this research is to develop a numerical model that accurately simulates the complex physical phenomena occurring in relativistic jets, incorporating the effects of the inverse Compton process and plasma instability. The simulation covers a large spatial scale, from the parsec to kiloparsec range, and accounts for the interaction between the jets and surrounding photons. The total energy emitted by the jets, as well as the regions where the inverse Compton process is most intense, can be identified and analyzed within the context of the observed radiation from multiple TeV sources. The energy balance between the jets and the photons is found to be highly dynamic, indicating a complex self-regulatory mechanism at work in the jets.

To address the limitations of the post-Newtonian series in general relativity, a more direct, pre-post-Newtonian framework is proposed. This pre-post-Newtonian scheme, built upon a distinct parameterization, enables an easier analytical expansion. This scheme employs a 'pre-non-relativistic' form of the metric, thereby eliminating certain relativistic effects, such as the pre-factor $c^{-2}$, which were inherent in the post-Newtonian approach. This parametric scheme, although novel, offers an alternative to general relativity, yet retains the ability to recover the standard post-Newtonian model when necessary. This pre-post-Newtonian framework, utilizing the gravitational potential in a self-consistent manner, paves the way for the derivation of the Schwarzschild solution through iterative processes.

SIFT-based methods are popular for registering SPECT/CT images due to their robustness in various conditions. However, the conventional approach combines feature matching with gradient optimization, which may not effectively register images with low contrast or local anomalies. To address this, we propose SIFT-CPD, which integrates the conventional method with optimal transport theory to directly optimize image alignment. Our proposed method demonstrates improved performance on synthetic images with realistic deformations and is validated on real medical data, including pediatric cardiac and abdominal/SPECT/CT images, and shows significant results in detecting fetal liver position.

A key technique in enhancing the robustness of deep learning models is the application of data transformation and weak strong augmentation frameworks. Recent approaches, however, have struggled to balance the complexity and efficiency of these methods, often resulting in a need for substantial memory resources. To address this challenge, we introduce the UOT-Pooling framework, a flexible and scalable method for generating diverse strong pseudo images. By leveraging optimal transport theory, our method can learn to map complex distributions and utilize trainable convolutional layers to generate strong images, all within the framework of UOT regularization. Experimental results demonstrate the remarkable effectiveness of our method, achieving a 0.6% improvement over the baseline on the ImageNet-1K dataset, and a 1.2% improvement over the D4FRA framework, which is one of the state-of-the-art methods, on the JODIS256 dataset. Notably, our method outperforms existing frameworks, including D4FRA, in terms of accuracy and F1-score, while also offering a more efficient and faster strong pseudo image generation process.

The structure of the galaxy's disk can influence the development of its active galactic nucleus (AGN). We analyzed the orientation of Seyfert galaxies with spiral patterns, focusing on the role of the galaxy's disk in shaping AGN development. We derived spiral patterns from the Galaxy Zoo dataset, and found a distinct difference in orientation between Type 1 and Type 2 Seyferts, particularly for intermediate to late spiral galaxies, where Type 1 Seyferts are more face-on and Type 2 Seyferts are more edge-on. This difference disappears in early spiral galaxies, indicating that the galaxy's disk structure plays a significant role in AGN development, with face-on disks favoring Type 1 Seyferts and early spiral galaxies allowing for both types.

This paper establishes a connection between a specific map and the characterization of flat general rotational surfaces, extending previous work that used the classical Gauss map. We provide a concrete example to demonstrate that our new map offers distinct advantages over the classical one, along with relevant theorem implications.

A key task in computer vision, image classification, has been extensively studied, particularly in relation to utilizing vast amounts of unlabeled data like ImageNet. However, utilizing such datasets for geometry pre-training has not been widely explored, largely due to the lack of explicit 3D information in images. To address this gap, we propose pre-training on scenes by extracting and leveraging detailed details from novel neural network representations, thereby enabling effective geometry estimation. Through comprehensive ablation studies and comparisons with established methods, including ImageNet, our proposed approach demonstrates superior performance on multiple benchmarks, ultimately enabling state-of-the-art results in novel view synthesis and indoor 6D pose estimation.

TCube is an innovative Time-Cube system developed to enhance the analysis of a single time-series by automatically generating visualizations and explanations.  By leveraging the Gröbner basis concept, TCube identifies and explains patterns in time-series data, providing a depth of insight beyond that of existing visual analytics tools.  By integrating a pattern matcher and symbolic reasoning engine, TCube can accurately assess whether time-series data fits specific patterns and accurately explain its behavior.  To compensate for the lack of comprehensive training data, TCube employs a symbolic approach that does not rely on pre-trained models.  As a result of its versatile design, TCube has the ability to adapt to various use-cases by allowing users to define their own patterns and evaluations using a high-level language.

The Ising model on a Cayley tree based on the $G(m,n)$ group allows for a detailed recursive analysis of the system's free energy levels. By utilizing the properties of the $G(m,n)$ group, a periodic transfer method is developed to track magnetization at various temperatures. Similarly, another iterative approach is created to examine susceptibility as the system moves through different temperature regimes, ultimately revealing the critical values in this process.

The geometric structure of phase space has significant implications for hyperbolic equations. This insight is developed here to understand the dynamics of wave breaking and the loss of solution regularity. By establishing a precise connection between the rate of metric contraction and the optimal time of smooth solution existence, we derive several key results. These include the criterion for smooth solution extension, the asymptotic behavior of solutions near singularities, and the precise behavior of hyperbolic equations as viscosity goes to zero. To achieve these outcomes, we introduce a novel, solution-dependent phase space metric that remains invariant under hyperbolic equation flow, along with other technical innovations.

This research introduces a novel application of Long Short-Term Memory networks to enhance Japanese word segmentation accuracy. By incorporating annotated words into the training process, our method successfully raises segmentation accuracy beyond baseline levels, aligning with real-world conditions. Additionally, we demonstrate that our results outperform previously proposed techniques, and we analyze various factors influencing the outcomes. Our work also explores how our proposed method performs at Japanese word boundary detection, and we present a comparison with existing approaches.

Stack Overflow, a widely utilized Q&A platform for coders, boasts a substantial body of external shared content in multiple forms, including references, snippets, and answers. Our investigation into this shared content reveals that references dominate it, accounting for 80.5% of all shared external resources. Additionally, our analysis of its utility shows that this content significantly aids Stack Overflow users, with 19.4% of posts requiring external content and contributors relying on it 30.1% of the time. Furthermore, our data shows that snippets are the external resource type with the highest degree of repeated sharing, while all types of external content are shared repetitively on average 1.5 to 2 times.
