We also develop a predictive model to estimate when nodes will be processed, and demonstrate the utility of clustering techniques to construct more efficient schedules for graph tasks. These innovations are seamlessly integrated into existing, widely-used GCN frameworks, and we assess their performance by evaluating the throughput improvements on sequential graph workflows on novel datasets, successfully increasing throughput by up to 2.17x.

Recent research on Trojan attacks on neural networks has highlighted their potential, yet it has been confined to crafting targeted training data. Our proposed method, called Trojan Attack using Training augmentation (TAT), innovatively integrates a synthetic data enhancement approach into model training, enabling a more practical and highly accurate alternative to previous targeted data methods. By utilizing this technique, our attack successfully achieves a substantial improvement in backdoor trigger activation rates (up to 97%) without incurring performance losses on clean data, providing a more viable option for real-world applications. Furthermore, the adaptable nature of our attack allows it to effectively function across diverse target models and trigger designs. Building upon our approach, we also develop a more efficient method, called Trojan Attack using Pseudo-labeling (TAL), which utilizes a semi-supervised learning framework using unlabeled data. Both attacks are rigorously tested on multiple targeted models, including VGG16, AdaNet, and Distillation, as well as various trigger designs, such as random, pattern, and Pico, with significant results on the ImageNet dataset.

ROSIE IFU, a recently installed instrument on the Australian Telescope Network, combines integral field unit technology with radio interferometry to provide detailed spatial information about specific regions in the sky. So far, it has been successfully used to create comprehensive maps of various celestial objects, such as nebulae, galaxies, and quasar jets, across a frequency range of 1.3 to 1.7 GHz. A recent upgrade has expanded its capabilities to include higher frequencies up to 2.3 GHz, which has enabled researchers to uncover previously hidden aspects of quasar jets and a nearby galaxy known as M81. Additionally, a new high-level mapping pipeline has significantly increased the speed of data processing and will soon be used to map a high-redshift galaxy to study the evolution of galaxies in the early universe. Additionally, a new feature has been introduced to the instrument, allowing for differential observations, which has led to the discovery of a strong magnetic field in a galaxy known as M82. Moreover, by using ROSIE IFU's detailed data, researchers have been able to model the structures of objects in the sky more accurately, which has enabled a more precise estimation of their total radio emission.

This study presents a novel, comprehensive theoretical model for calculating low-energy astrophysical $S$-factors, specifically tailored to p-wave reactions. The existing quantum mechanical frameworks are modified to develop this model, which effectively accounts for sub-barential reactions. The proposed approach offers a straightforward, direct model for computing sub-barential cross-sections, which can be efficiently integrated into computational methods. The standard Coulomb wave functions are replaced with the ground state proton wave function, resulting in the development of the model. The results from this model are validated by comparing it to experimental data on the $^{19}$F(p,$\gamma$)$^{20}$Ne $S$-factor, showcasing excellent agreement. The computational model is then applied to calculate sub-barential $S$-factors for various nuclei, including $^{13}$C, $^{15}$O, $^{17}$F, $^{21}$Ne, $^{25}$Mg, $^{29}$P, $^{31}$O, $^{37}$Cl, $^{39}$K, $^{43}$Sc, $^{47}$Mn, and $^{63}$Cu.

Researchers have identified a large number of small planets orbiting stars similar to our Sun, similar in size to Earth, which are located within the habitable zones of their respective stars. These stars, a subset of which is observed by TESS, are relatively calm and pose a lower risk of atmospheric erosion due to reduced flaring. We propose a model for determining the interior structures and mineral composition of such planets, using the example of an example of a planet within the habitable zone of a quiet Sun-like star. We demonstrate that a planet with the same mass and radius as Earth, but situated around a quiet Sun-like star, would have a significantly larger core and a smaller mantle compared to Earth, which is likely to result in a more Mars-like core-mantle structure. We also find that planets with radii under 1.5 Earth radii, similar to the stars observed by TESS, are more likely to have a significant iron core and a thinner mantle. These findings suggest that such planets would have different tectonic activities and volcanic activities, which would have a significant impact on their potential atmospheres and potential for life.

This paper addresses the issue of channel capacity limitations in distributed MIMO systems and proposes an attention-based channel information method to enhance data transmission. 
Specifically, this study investigates the efficacy of attention mechanisms in learning relevant features from channel information in a message-passing massive MIMO framework. 
The proposed method leverages attention to develop an efficient and adaptive learning process for Channel State Information in a multi-user MIMO system. 
The channel encoder and decoder are developed as a multi-task neural network and optimized using multi-task stochastic gradient descent. 
The results from numerical evaluations confirm that the attention-based feature learning is effective and that the multi-task neural network can efficiently manage various tasks while minimizing resource allocation.

This study offers a systematic approach by integrating modern category theory with the semantics of topological T_0 logic, building on the initial research of Hales in the 1970s. Our primary goal is to demonstrate how generalizing from topological spaces to topological categories provides a more comprehensive framework for understanding the semantics of the logic. By doing so, we not only offer a more intuitive interpretation of Hales' pioneering work but also establish a robust foundation for the formalization of spatial operations within this context. Ultimately, our research lays the groundwork for a more thorough exploration of the space preservation operations that the logic can express.

In 1990, Kotzig and Tuttle proposed the idea that every bipartite graph with a maximum degree of 3 can be strong edge-colored using at most $m+1$ colors, where $m$ is the number of edges. This theory has since been refined, yielding a question by 1999 in which it was determined that the upper limit for the number of colors needed is actually at most $\Delta + 3$, where $\Delta$ represents the maximum degree of the graph. A variant of the problem was also considered in which the edge-coloring condition was changed to allow adjacent vertices to have different edge colors, resulting in the total number of colors needed being not more than $\Delta + 2$. Both scenarios were explored and it was found that large, bipartite graphs with a maximum degree of 3 require at least $\Delta + 1$ colors when considering the original problem, and at least $\Delta + 2$ colors when considering the modified version.

The concept of support for functions within eigenspaces of Hamming graphs enables the generalization of classical results for projective planes and finite fields to cases with non-prime fields. This paper presents a study on the minimal support size for functions within specific eigenspaces of Hamming graphs. Key findings reveal that the minimum support size adheres to certain inequalities under various conditions, such as when $i$ is less than or equal to $1$ or when $i$ and $j$ meet specific requirements, resulting in conditions like $(q-1)^2$ or $(q-1)^3$. Notably, these findings align with previously established bounds, but also present new instances where such bounds apply, including a new occurrence of the eigenspace bound for $P_{q^2}^2(2)$ within $\mathcal{E}_1^{(2)}(q)$.

COPASI is a leading platform for analyzing systems biology models, widely used in the community for its versatility. To leverage COPASI's capabilities on web platforms, an existing API was found insufficient due to its limitation in handling authentication and session management. Consequently, ShinyCOPASI was developed as a R/Shiny extension, enabling model evaluation, data extraction, and script execution through a web interface, while also providing a secure API using HTTP cookies for authentication. Furthermore, ShinyCOPASI API capabilities are API-capable, allowing integration with external programs through a Shiny web interface.

Recent advancements in neural networks have led to significant breakthroughs in addressing complex inverse problems and problems that are inherently unstable. Traditionally, these issues have been tackled using robust, data-driven methods, but now a data-driven approach using neural networks has gained attention for their efficiency and versatility. This paper provides an overview of various types of neural network architectures that have emerged to solve inverse problems and a problem framework for analyzing their convergence in theoretical terms. We conduct detailed theoretical analyses and numerical experiments to evaluate the convergence properties of different architectures within a specific problem setting - deconvolution. Our comprehensive comparison highlights the strengths and limitations of these models, ultimately providing valuable insights for future research directions.

The algebra of class functions for a quantum group, such as $SU_q(2)$, $U_q(2)$, or $S_q(3)$, is shown to form a particularly comprehensive and self-similar subset of its C*-algebra. This key finding is then leveraged to establish the existence of extensive collections of MASA's within these specific C*-algebras, containing a measureable element from each equivalence class of irreducible representations, which contains a measureable element from each equivalence class of irreducible representations, ultimately leading to the existence of a measureable element from each equivalence class of irreducible representations, including elements representing each irreducible representation.

Traditional dynamic programming approaches, which involve exhaustive searches for optimal policies, are often impractical due to their high computational demands. As a result, many researchers have turned to iterative methods to find a better policy incrementally. Although iterative policy evaluation can be done inexactly to save time, this may lead to substantial overall computation. This study presents an application of GMRES, an iterative method, to dynamic programming for Markov decision processes (MDPs) with bounded rewards. By using noisy policy evaluations, we show that IGMRES, an inexact version of the method, converges to an accurate solution. Computational experiments reveal that GMRES policy iteration converges to a precise solution in just 10 iterations for an MDP with 100,000 states, approximately 10 times faster than traditional policy iteration. Furthermore, incorporating BICG as a preconditioner for GMRES results in a significant improvement, allowing it to surpass IGMRES by being roughly 500 times faster.

In a more general context of oriented graphs, specifically those assigned with orientation and weighting, this research delves into the comparison of symbolic and ordinary powers of edge ideals, taking into consideration the degrees of vertices. We establish conditions under which the equality of all n-th symbolic and ordinary powers of an edge ideal holds, and we also define and studied a broader version of the Delta Delta Delta property for coverings, specifically Delta Delta Delta property for complete link coverings, and provide examples to demonstrate the effectiveness of our given conditions.

To facilitate high-level programming of computer simulators, we suggest an approach that involves using a translator to automatically convert scripts written in a high-level language into an equivalent code in the simulator's original code. This method could be particularly useful in exploring large parameter spaces, as it is widely utilized, as well as in solving inverse problems. By allowing users to write simpler and more readable code, this approach significantly decreases the likelihood of errors and shortens the development time. We demonstrate this method's effectiveness using the TSUNAMI code for the purpose of optimizing a reactor model.

This research investigates the feasibility of robust learning when concept parameters are variable and uncertain, and we define a model with a specified radius that represents the maximum distance between parameters within different distributions. We investigate whether a fixed radius allows for robust learning without assumptions about the concept distribution, and we find that distribution-free robust learning is impossible for a fixed radius but possible when the radius is related to the maximum variation in the concept parameters. Additionally, we derive a bound on the sample size needed to learn when the radius is variable, and we show that our bound is optimal for certain concept classes by comparing it to a fixed radius bound.

Our study investigates how initial conditions affect the production of jets accompanied by isolated photons at mid-rapidity. By comparing these scenarios to measurements obtained at the LHC, we can assess the accuracy of the models. Additionally, our research delves into the connection between isolated photons and jets, particularly in terms of their impact on parton momentum distributions. This connection allows us to gain insights into joint distributions that are beyond the reach of photon-less processes.

We show that a specific evaluation of an alternating Apéry series involving powers can be expressed as an intersection of the set $\mathbb{Q}[\zeta(3),\zeta(2k),\zeta(4k),k\geq1]$ and the set $I=\bigcap_{k\geq1}\{\zeta(2k),\zeta(4k)\}$. As a result, calculating the irrationally independent elements in this alternating Apéry expansion requires a smaller subset of multiple zeta values compared to the non-alternating version. Furthermore, we establish a rational relationship between the alternating and non-alterminating Apéry expansions with exponents up to 6. Employing Waldschmidt's criterion, we prove the linear independence over $\mathbb{Q}$ of specific irrationals derived from $\pi$ and $G$.

The primary goal of this research is to accurately determine the distance, speed, and direction of WISE 1508+1378, a rapidly moving brown dwarf with an unusual trajectory, by combining measurements of its radial velocity and infrared spectrum from the SOAR and Keck telescopes. With these observations in hand, we were able to confirm that data from the Gaia satellite correctly identifies this object as stationary in three-dimensional space. Furthermore, we determined that WISE 1508+1378 is approximately 16 parsecs away from us, making it the eighth closest brown dwarf to the solar system. We analyzed spectral data in detail and discovered evidence that this object shares characteristics with several other rapidly moving stars, suggesting a shared origin in the local population of velocity near the sun, local associations of the sun, often referred to as the 'Moving Groups'. We used these findings to establish a preliminary age estimate for WISE 1508+1378, assuming it formed at the same time as other nearby stars, which would make it approximately 300 million to 800 million years old.

Our research on high-energy collision events, such as those involving protons, light ions, and nuclei, reveals interesting patterns in the creation of particles and their antiparticles. In smaller collision events, we see an increase in the amount of $\bar{\textup{p}}/\textup{p}$ and $\bar{\textup{p}}/\Lambda$ particles, along with a decrease in the $\Lambda/\textup{p}$ particles, which differs significantly from what is observed in heavier collision events. Additionally, we found an overall increase in the $\bar{\Lambda}$ particles, $\bar{\Lambda}/\Lambda$, and $\bar{\Lambda}/\textup{p}$ particles as event size increases. These particles' patterns suggest a relationship between event multiplicity and the matter-antimatter imbalance, which becomes less pronounced in larger systems. In an attempt to reconcile these results with theoretical models, we discovered that $\bar{\Lambda}$ particles appear to follow the same patterns as $\bar{\textup{p}}$ particles, which our models can accurately predict across all measured event classes.

We're examining the double parton distribution functions at a particular scale in the large-x regime, using the background field formalism. This approach not only yields results for any scale but also provides a pathway to understanding the function at the confinement scale. Double parton distribution functions are more intricate than their single parton distribution function counterparts due to their dependence on the positions of two partons. This added complexity is further exemplified by constraints imposed by PT-symmetry. Our work focuses on deriving PT-symmetry relations for the functions involving two valence partons in the large-x limit, specifically considering the scenarios where the partons are either external or internal.

This research delves into the properties and applications of Martian and Lunar soil (regolith) materials through experimental analysis and computational simulation. To achieve this, 3D printing was used to create regolith samples, which were then subjected to various testing methods including micro-CT scanning, mechanical stress evaluation, and surface examination using Scanning Electron Microscopy. Our findings suggest that Martian and Lunar soil have significant potential for use in space construction and additive manufacturing. Specifically, 3D printing was successful with both types of materials, which performed similarly to each other, with some variations. Our research highlights the advantages of using polymeric and metal inks in combination with regolith to produce high-quality, extruded material. These findings have implications for future space missions, particularly in supporting human exploration of the Moon and Mars by enabling advanced in-situ resource utilization techniques.

We examine the behaviour of a thin liquid film on a fibrous surface that is inclined relative to gravity, under conditions where the surface has a variable slip property. This study utilizes two distinct methods to analyze the formation of drops in such systems, focusing on cases where the surface slip is above and below a critical threshold. Above the critical slip value, we utilize numerical techniques to model the steady-state behaviour of the liquid film, revealing the universal characteristics of emerging unstable non-uniform patterns. Conversely, below this threshold, we utilize an analytical approach to demonstrate that drops consistently form through a sequence of bifurcations, provided that the surface slip varies sufficiently rapidly.

By combining the Prospector Bayesian inference framework with observed UV to optical spectroscopy data from six star-forming galaxies, this work leverages the concept of $\beta$ luminosity to evaluate star formation rate (SFR) accuracy. Prospector's versatility in modeling stellar populations and physical conditions, alongside its capacity to quantify uncertainty through broad posterior distributions, makes it an ideal tool for galaxy modeling. Using a synthetic dataset to validate its reliability, we applied our framework to observe real star-forming galaxy data in the local universe. By comparing our model to an independent UV to optical spectroscopy measurement of SFR, we utilized $\beta$ luminosity to assess our framework's accuracy. Our study reveals a slight overestimation of SFR in galaxies exhibiting high $\beta$ luminosity, yet within acceptable error margins, we establish that Prospector effectively captures star-forming galaxies' physical properties and stellar population dynamics.

In this study, a surprising link between quadratic categories and exceptional braided auto-equivalences of categories orbifiled by a specific category is discovered, resulting in the creation of an influential link model. The derived category of a unique symmetric group and an alternative method of obtaining this connection through a Galois super-orbifold approach are additionally explored, which leads to the solution of long-standing open problems in the field.

This study examines stochastic perturbation of the Fisher-KPP equation, a model used to describe how a beneficial trait spreads within a population. By applying random noise to this deterministic model, we investigate the behavior of the resulting population front. Initially, in a confined area, the population front expands at a speed that aligns with the speed of a wave. However, beyond a certain point, the front's growth pattern shifts, now resembling a faster, linear progression. Furthermore, analyzing the deterministic model's solution reveals its smooth properties and how the probability measure of this model converges over time, following the established profile, along the line representing the front's growth.

This paper outlines our approach to tackling the UbiComp 2021 Challenge, focusing on detecting written activities using solely time-based sensor information, without any visual component. Our method relies on previously effective techniques employing the FFT algorithm to differentiate periods of written and non-written states. We then employ the Dynamic Time Warping algorithm to analyze the extracted frequency signals and classify the written content into four four-letter categories by comparing unknown words with four pre-established frequency signatures. Our experiments with the provided dataset yielded accurate results, with a high classification accuracy of around 85%.

The conventional method models a duration distribution as having constant parameters, but our novel approach recognizes that these parameters vary, and utilizes additional variables to represent their changes, and a probabilistic framework, and potential improvements in the accuracy of future duration predictions can be quantified, and this was successfully applied to model the duration of soccer matches.

Occupancy modeling, a widely used statistical method in ecology, is often applied to detect species presence using sensor data such as acoustic recordings, camera traps, or genetic samples. The occurrence of each species is modeled as a binary state, but estimating correlations between species' occurrences can be computationally burdensome due to the large scale of these models. A novel Bayesian framework for multivariate occupancy modeling, acORAM, combines Robbins-Rasmussen asymptotic reasoning with the Adams-Gaussian process framework to model species' occurrences, taking advantage of the conjugate prior setup with a multin-Logit regression result. By assuming exchangeable observations, the model can be analyzed using variational inference, which, as demonstrated through simulations, results in more efficient computation, especially in evaluations using real-world data from bird songs, plant seeds, and mammal movements.

The Skincare project involves developing an intelligent diagnostic and adaptive learning system for skin cancer, designed to augment the skills of medical professionals and augment existing medical education tools.

To achieve this goal, the project is developing advanced machine learning algorithms that can analyze visual data and provide accurate assessments, as well as adaptive learning tools for doctors to develop personalized treatment strategies.

A large annotated dataset has been compiled for training and evaluating these algorithms, along with interactive tools for medical staff to prioritize and discuss individual cases.

Initially, the project focused on melanoma, but now plans to expand its capabilities for broader skin condition detection.

Ia supernovae are crucial for measuring large-scale structures in the universe, but their individual properties can introduce significant uncertainties in measurements. This study explores how machine learning models can be used to reduce the impact of this unmodeled variability on cosmological measurements. By incorporating a correlation-related cost into the training process, our model successfully captures the diversity of Type Ia supernovae and their redshift distribution. This approach enhances the reliability of the model without compromising its accuracy, and combined with improved data quality, it has the potential to yield more precise cosmological measurements.

Observations of a starburst galaxy, located 110 megaparsecs away in the direction of the constellation Hydra, were conducted using a millimeter-wave spectrograph. These observations revealed the presence of significant molecular gas outflows, spreading across more than 100,000 light-years from the galaxy's center, and extending over a wide frequency range equivalent to the speed of light. Analysis of the data indicates that the mass of gas leaving the galaxy at a rate of 0.18 to 0.23 solar masses per year per unit of star formation, and within the region of outflows, the gas moves at a speed of 300 to 350 kilometers per second. These outflows are likely a result of a supernova-driven feedback process that is expelling gas and may be preventing the formation of new stars in the galaxy.

The behavior of particle-laden plumes has been investigated through numerical simulations, examining the impact of particles on plume scaling, especially in the self-similar zone, by solving the equations of motion for both fluid and particle phases. These studies vary the amount of entrained mass and the ratio of plume and particle buoyancy fluxes. When particles' downdrafts exceed their downdrafts, an increase in entrainment is observed, which can be attributed to an enhanced conversion of kinetic energy into potential energy for both phases due to an increased downdraft area. Conversely, when particles' downdrafts are weaker, an decrease in entrainment is observed, along with the development of large, persistent voids near the plume's leading edge that decrease the conversion of kinetic energy into potential energy due to an increased downdraft area.

Generalizing graph models of contagion, we've developed a hypergraph model to simulate how a contagion spreads through populations. The model incorporates the effects of population dynamics, where individuals change their states based on their connections to others. Unlike traditional models, our model doesn't always follow the same patterns when the model type changes from one to another, such as from Susceptible-Susceptible to Susceptible-Infected models. However, by utilizing results from percolation theory in models where the infection rate is very low, we were able to establish a universal method to calculate the infection rate for a wide range of models.

By applying a magnetic field, researchers have successfully manipulated the domain wall configuration in a Fe/Mn/Fe bilayer system, and observed the impact of mechanical strain on the domain wall structure through transmission electron microscopy. This control allowed for examination of how strain affects the domain wall's domain polarization and spin configuration, and revealed a correlation between the two under strain. Additionally, mechanical stress was found to affect the domain wall's domain polarization, influencing its electronic transport properties in the iron layers of the sample. This discovery has significant implications for the development of spintronic devices that utilize domain walls for their unique conduction characteristics, particularly those featuring non-ferromagnetic materials with topological transport properties.

Our study builds upon the framework of a preceding investigation, where we developed an advanced dynamo model accounting for the indirect influence of stellar rotation on magnetic activity through kinematic and dynamo modes. In this report, we present a significant enhancement of the code's performance, particularly in terms of memory efficiency, enabling simulations across extended time periods. Utilizing this upgraded code, we conducted an expansive exploration of the parameter space for two star models, focusing on the effects of stellar rotation and magnetic diffusion. As a result, we observed the occurrence of magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars, displaying characteristics analogous to the Sun, and discovered that at lower rotation speeds, the dynamos exhibit characteristics more akin to stationary wave-like patterns, and show increased susceptibility to magnetic mode switches. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of magnetic diffusion on the operation of the dynamos, and discovered that for sufficiently high diffusion rates, magnetic cycles cease to occur, and the modes shift to stationary states, and the likelihood of mode-switching increases.

We introduce a novel model that integrates task relationships in learning tasks with multiple inputs and outputs, allowing it to make independent task predictions while also capturing their inherent connections. This method employs a shared feature extractor that generates specific task characteristics, which are then utilized by multiple output-specific classifiers. Our approach enables the sharing of task information, which in turn enhances the accuracy of multiple学习任务. Experimental results on multiple learning tasks and multiple-related tasks show that the proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art models, particularly when it comes to handling independent tasks. Moreover, the method exhibits a high level of interpretability by explicitly modeling task-related characteristics, thus providing a clear understanding of task connections.

The McMini model checker, a speed-optimized version of Trelbrax's PVS-based model checker, focuses on efficiently verifying complex multi-threaded operations. We enhance McMini's performance by integrating an in-place integer sorting algorithm and an optimized thread-scheduling approach, resulting in increased capacity to verify the correctness of these operations. Our results show McMini's time efficiency surpasses CPASERVER, an advanced integer-programming-based model checker, by at least a factor of ten on various thread operations. Additionally, we present new records on the complexity of verifying nested nested CC calls and nested compare-and-swaps, establishing lower bounds that reflect the computational challenges posed by these operations.

Recently, misinformation has been shown to cause significant harm in various real-world situations, leading to increased interest in understanding how to address it. As a major messaging platform, WhatsApp has shown a significant presence in disseminating misinformation, prompting the company to take action by implementing new features to detect and limit the spread of potentially misleading information. Although WhatsApp has not provided a detailed explanation of its approach, our research aims to uncover and analyze its mechanism by creating a publicly available dataset, which is the first of its kind, consisting of approximately 1000 suspicious groups out of a total of 5000 examined. By examining WhatsApp's feature, we have developed a classifier that effectively identifies suspicious groups with an accuracy rate of 78.6%, surpassing the performance of comparable classifiers in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

This paper presents an in-depth analysis of interactions within a population model that accommodates two key characteristics: genetic diversity and the concept of friends. The effect of mutations on population evolution, modeled as random events, significantly impacts genetic diversity, whereas the dynamics of friendships have minimal effect on this aspect. Conversely, introducing friendships has a notable impact on population structure, leading to distinct differences compared to populations lacking these relationships. Moreover, simulations reveal that the effects of friendships and mutations interact in a non-trivial manner, thereby influencing population structure in a complex way. Our findings demonstrate that it is feasible to differentiate between simulations incorporating genetic changes and those featuring friendships based on population variability and structure.

A novel speech countermeasure, based on pre-trained neural networks, is presented to detect spoofed audio. This approach, Pre-trained Neural Network with Attention for Spoocoverboos, integrates attention mechanisms at both the block and channel levels to enhance performance. We have implemented this method on top of ResNet, and evaluated its efficacy on large collections of spoofed and genuine voices, specifically the NIST SPK-OVERBOOBS dataset. Through a series of experiments, we have demonstrated that the integration of attention mechanisms significantly improves the area under the curve of the equal error rate for audio spoofing detection, and notably, the area under the curve increased by 10.3% compared to the model without attention mechanisms. Furthermore, this method demonstrates enhanced generalizability when tested on unseen datasets, outperforming alternative approaches in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

This review summarizes the relationship between supergravity, low-energy theoretical models, and quantum gravity, as well as the various theoretical and mathematical challenges that arise from connecting these frameworks. The findings and insights reported in related research are presented, with an emphasis on the implications of supergravity's relationship to string theory.

The coherence of photonic states is crucial for developing complex systems of light that can process and store data. We investigated the coherence functions of two-photon and four-photon states produced in a silicon microdisk. By reversing the direction of the pump beam, we were able to observe distinct patterns of coherence functions, indicating a unique photoassociation effect. The observed coherence functions align with predictions based on PHARA, a theoretical model predicting four-photon state correlations in time. Our findings are further validated by an analytical calculation, demonstrating the effectiveness of our predicted coherence functions.

In this paper, two types of silicon materials, namely Etched Silicon (ES) and buffer oxide etched silicon (EOES), are investigated in terms of their electrical properties. The EOES material, a recently introduced technique, involves using an oxide layer as a buffer to stabilize the silicon substrate prior to etching, leading to the formation of a distinct region between the silicon substrate and the ES layer. The carrier concentration in EOES silicon was found to be significantly higher than that in conventional ES silicon. The carrier concentration in EOES silicon was determined using the Four Point Probe method and found to meet the requirements for forward bias operation. The ES and EOES silicon materials were tested for diode characteristics, and the results showed that the ES silicon material exhibited ideal diode behavior with a saturation current of $10^{-14}$ A, while the EOES silicon material exhibited a saturation current of $10^{-10}$ A. The ES and EOES silicon materials were also tested for transistor operation, and the results showed that the ES silicon material exhibited a current gain of $100$, while the EOES silicon material exhibited a current gain of $10$. The results of this study indicate that the ES silicon material is suitable for VLSI applications, while the EOES silicon material may be suitable for analog circuit applications.

A recent research paper explored whether partitioning a set into specific subsets with certain properties (like being closed or continuous sets) affects the possible ways a set can be divided. The paper showed that a set can be split into closed sets in significantly more ways than it can be split into those same type of subsets. The paper's findings led to a natural question about other types of subsets, specifically monotone subsets of the real line, in what follows we demonstrate that a set can be split into these subsets in significantly more ways than it can be split into closed or continuous sets. The shown result relies on the assumption that certain advanced mathematical concepts like the Generalized Continuum Hypothesis are true. The proven result also has implications for other types of subsets, like bounded sets or sets defined using the Borel properties. The shown result implies that a set can be split into these types of subsets in significantly more ways than it can be split into closed or continuous sets, in situations where the concept of independence from the Continuum Hypothesis is relevant. The shown result also has applications in defining functions that map points on a line to sets defined using the Borel properties in infinitely many different dimensions of space. The proven result implies that a set can be split into these types of subsets in infinitely many different ways when considering higher dimensions of space. The shown result also has implications for defining functions that map points on a line to sets defined using measures in higher dimensions of space. The shown result implies

This paper delves into the concept of short-term reversal trading, a strategy linked to various behavioral theories such as overconfidence and loss aversion. By reexamining the strategy through a rational framework, our research finds that short-term reversal traders' actions can be effectively mimicked by commodity trading advisors, whose performance is often measured by notable events like the Commodore's Week. Consequently, a mutually beneficial relationship may exist between short-term reversal traders and CTA, as their shared interests lie in the manipulation of market perceptions and behavior.

A notable issue with current network workloads is the vulnerability of network monitoring tools. This problem is exacerbated by a phenomenon known as "Silent Evasion", where malicious traffic successfully bypasses detection systems. To tackle this challenge, researchers proposed "Dynamic Protocol Detection" (DPC), a mechanism designed to identify complex protocols even when they manipulate field lengths to hide their content. However, it remains uncertain how effective this mechanism is against attacks designed to exploit its weaknesses. This research addresses this gap by creating three attacks that manipulate the input of network tools to bypass the DPC mechanism. These successful attacks demonstrate that existing network tools can be vulnerable to the "Silent Evasion" technique, effectively ignoring malicious traffic. As such, this research calls for a need for more robust network monitoring tools that can withstand such attacks and reliably detect suspicious activity.

Our method allows for the calculation of how magnons propagate in magnetic films near superconducting structures. This method utilizes Green's functions and incorporates the boundary conditions that arise from the Meissner effect. This effective approach effectively models the impact of superconducting walls on magnon propagation, eliminating the need for computationally intensive micromagnetic simulations. This efficient algorithm can be scaled up to simulate larger systems comprising numerous atomic layers. This method's effectiveness was verified by comparing its predictions of magnon propagation in a magnetic film near a superconducting strip with predictions from less efficient micromagnetic simulations. This methodology promises to significantly reduce simulation times for analyzing magnon behavior in large systems, potentially consisting of up to $10^5$ atomic layers.

Recent advancements in federated learning have primarily focused on enhancing privacy protection, but the method faces challenges when dealing with diverse and unique data sets held by participating clients. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel, distribution-robust approach to federated learning that necessitates minimal assumptions about the shift in distribution across devices. Our approach leverages an efficient local augmentation technique that generates synthetic data samples, thereby ensuring alignment of the global model with local models and preventing model drift. Notably, our strategy is versatile, versatile, versatile, versatile, and does not require modifications to the standard federated learning process. Experimental evaluations on various tasks demonstrate the significant improvement in classification performance achieved by our approach. Consequently, we contend that this approach can be effectively employed in real-world federated learning scenarios where data is inherently non-identical and non-independent.

A crucial operation in quantum information processing is the quantum Fourier transform (QFT), yet its extension to high-dimensional systems has not been thoroughly explored. Here, we introduce a quantum circuit utilizing a beam splitter to perform the QFT on two-photon states across high-dimensional dimensions. We demonstrate its application in implementing a Grover search within an HD system, showing faster search speeds compared to a base algorithm. Furthermore, we utilize the QFT to develop an enhanced error correction technique, achieving more accurate corrections in complex, high-dimensional states. Our findings highlight the value of increased dimensionality for applications in quantum computation and communication.

In a non-line-of-sight environment with an installed Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS), channel estimation is typically done by splitting it into two parts, which often results in increased overhead and decreased accuracy. This research aims to address these limitations by introducing an optimization-based technique that jointly estimates the combined effect of the direct and reflected channel coefficients. This joint estimation utilizes known pilot signals at the receiver and introduces an optimization framework. By leveraging the properties of the combined channel, the proposed method achieves significant reductions in estimation error, which outperforms traditional approaches that separately estimate the channels, and also demonstrates substantial savings in pilot signal requirements, which is a critical factor in enhancing spectral efficiency.

The study examined how US local news outlets reported on the COVID-19 pandemic, including coverage of related deaths, through an examination of online content from 142 stations between February 2020 and March 2021. Content was analyzed using both machine learning algorithms and human coders to assess prominence, relevance to public health, and overall coverage volume. These findings were then used to explore associations with community characteristics, including COVID-19 mortality rates, community size, political leaning, and access to healthcare resources. Machine learning models revealed that news volume and public health focus were influenced by community population, COVID-19 mortality, and healthcare accessibility. Content analysis showed an increase in public health focus over time, with machine learning models predicting a corresponding decrease in overall coverage volume during the same period.

Counting is an intuitive skill that infants and young children掌握, but its development across species and over time offers a unique platform for investigation into the neural basis of counting. Recent studies in machine learning have yielded similar findings, prompting an exploration of the relationship between the progression of counting in humans and the progression of machine learning models in counting. Through experiments, we discovered that both human children and machine models exhibit similarities in counting progression, yet also show distinct differences. Specifically, models were found to be able to count beyond their training limits through systematic extrapolation. Furthermore, we observed that during learning, models initially count sequentially but eventually begin skipping numbers when approaching their capacity limit. The number skipped correlates with prior training experiences. Additionally, models were able to reduce the magnitude of skipped numbers through additional extrapolation training. These findings highlight potential benefits of using systematic extrapolation as a strategy to enhance model transferability.

We introduce xor filters, an innovative data structure that quickly and efficiently determines whether an item is likely a new entry or part of an existing collection of unique items in a limited amount of memory. Xor filters are optimized versions of Bloom filters, an space-efficient method for storing large sets of items, which can be used as the foundation for building databases capable of handling billions of items on a single device. Xor filters reduce the number of operations needed to verify an item and minimize the number of false positives, making them faster and more space-efficient than traditional Bloom filters. Our research demonstrates that for the same error rate, xor filters are up to 1.4 times faster and 30% more space-efficient than Bloom filters, a significant time savings of tens of milliseconds on mobile devices. Additionally, an implementation of the algorithm is available online at https://github.com/kevinbaxter/xorfilter.

This article establishes a direct connection between the Alexandrov body construction and divisorial Zariski decomposition, drawing parallels to earlier work by Bonavero and Serrano. Furthermore, it defines the divisorial Serrano decomposition for minimal models that may not be strictly projective, and explores the properties of such models in relation to their corresponding Alexandrov bodies.

The time frame in which market information is available changes constantly, suggesting that current price data can't always be used to make profitable decisions within that same time frame, as lag may occur. Our study aims to determine the extent to which past transaction data can help predict the length of informational lag. By applying a novel approach known as change point detection to the order flow of the Bitcoin market, based on data from Upbit between 2017 and 2021, we found strong evidence that the factors influencing informational lag are consistently predictable using the principles of effective market hypothesis, particularly at shorter time frames. Our results are supported by visual analysis and additional statistical tests, and we have tested the generalizability of our approach on order flow datasets from the S&P 500 and NASDAQ 100 indices, with successful results across both directional and volatility time scales.

FLVoogd, a FL-based clustering framework, protects privacy when creating groups of similar items while preventing a centralized control. By using Bayesian inference on Bayesian neural networks, it groups items that share characteristics without revealing their specific details. During training, data is applied to update the network's knowledge, which is then used through approximate binary search to determine cluster identities. To improve performance, FLVoogd utilizes a binary indexing mechanism, benefiting from existing data relationships and reducing querying costs. Various experiments demonstrate that exchanging model parameters in FLVoogd results in better or comparable outcomes compared to conventional clustering methods using traditional communication methods.

The 2021 Grand Challenge of the Autonomous Vehicle Development Alliance showcased state-of-the-art techniques in autonomous vehicle development, with particular focus on sim2real transfer. This report highlights key findings from a review of submissions, noting that many achieved high performance in evaluation metrics but struggled with effective generalization. Notably, certain approaches demonstrated low performance when tested in disparate environments. Our analysis also identified areas for improvement and proposed avenues for further research.

The growing sophistication of deepfake media has sparked significant concern about the widespread dissemination of deceptive information. A key factor driving this issue is the dissemination of information through a vast network of interconnected online platforms, often referred to as the 'information ecosystem'. While existing research has analyzed misinformation within individual sites, there is a pressing need to extend this analysis across various online environments. To address this gap, we have developed a multi-step approach that involves identifying key online spaces, tracking misinfomarkers within them, and monitoring their interactions. By applying this framework to Twitter and Reddit, we have found substantial overlaps in the content shared across these platforms, revealing complex patterns of misinformation dissemination. Our findings also highlight variations in user behavior and the influence of site-specific features on misinfomarkers' longevity.

We have developed two models to analyze the atmospheric composition of temperate planets around M-dwarf stars, considering both small and massive atmospheres, whether they represent an outflowing volcanic plume or an ancient crustal residue. Our research employs temperature and pressure data from volcanic planets Glieze-6379 and Earth, as well as pressure variability from temperature data, to understand atmospheric composition. Our results indicate significant variations in a small atmosphere, particularly in temperature, pressure, and chemical composition, whereas a massive atmosphere exhibits uniform properties. A small planet with volcanic activity is unlikely to have a carbon-based or water-rich atmosphere, making it an unsuitable candidate for life, whereas a massive planet's atmosphere is more likely to be water-rich and potentially carbon-based, with high surface temperatures rendering it uninhabitable.

The classic Hopfield network serves as a robust foundation for association learning and pattern completion.  Although research has explored the application of the Hopfield network for semantic memory, its learning process remains confined to Hebbian learning and limited to learning single associations.  To address these shortcomings, a modified McCulloch-Pitts network is proposed, developing an associative semantic memory that can be dynamically updated through continuous semantic learning, leveraging both batch learning and online learning methods enabled by gradient descent.  The adaptability of the network allows it to integrate diverse mathematical models, including the Gating Hopfield network, BFGP, and multi-layered patterns of activation, while maintaining transparency in its updates.  By comparing the network to the human hippocampus, the network exhibits pattern separation capabilities akin to the dentate gyrus, demonstrating superior performance on standard semantic memory tasks attributed to the human hippocampus.

Neural network-based computer vision models have revolutionized the accuracy of text recognition outside of the laboratory. Out-of-vocabulary (OOV) datasets have been instrumental in further improving model performance through widespread data collection and annotation. However, a lack of detailed annotations in datasets hinders researchers from gaining a deeper understanding of data characteristics and their potential applications. To address this limitation, we introduce a comprehensive analysis of data sets, which reveals critical insights into data and highlights underexplored areas. Leveraging our insights, we propose a novel technique for generalizing text synthesis, which can create previously unseen words based on existing data. This could lead to significant advancements in scene text recognition by enabling models to better adapt and improve performance.

Isolated branches of numerical solutions can be effectively found using a novel Newton-type method based on interval arithmetic, which finds significant applications in computing critical points and bifurcations in complex systems such as those involved in fluid dynamics. This algorithm utilizes interval operators to rigorously confirm unbounded asymptotic solutions and can adapt to various problems through customizable operators. Furthermore, a corresponding implementation is available in multiple languages including Julia, Java, and Python, with precomputed libraries for specific problems like the Ginzburg-Landau model and the Ginzburg-Landau-Stewart model.

Machine learning performance change point detection and failure mode isolation methods have seen increased interest in the literature. However, a challenge arises due to the high computational demands of these methods, which render them impractical in settings with a limited number of data points. To overcome this limitation, we present novel, efficient algorithms designed for resource-constrained environments. These algorithms demonstrate improved accuracy compared to existing methods while requiring only a fraction of the time in terms of computational complexity. To achieve this, we propose an adaptive method for selecting a suitable distance metric and incorporate a technique to filter out irrelevant data features in order to enhance performance and accuracy. Moreover, we introduce methods for feature selection aimed at identifying the most significant failure modes, which in turn improve the accuracy of failure mode isolation and facilitate more effective feature extraction. The proposed methods are validated through comprehensive numerical experiments and case studies conducted on real-world data sets, which demonstrate their effectiveness and efficiency.

Our previous examination of radial velocity and metallicity data from the Gaia survey revealed two large, distinct structures within the Gaia-Sausage Enceladus (GSE) system, referred to as the blue and red GSE groups, hinting at possible internal separation processes within its host galaxy. To further investigate this pattern, we analyzed additional chemical elements including iron, magnesium, calcium, and sodium in the same system, along with an unrelated dwarf galaxy Wukong (WUK), another group linked to the Milky Way. We found that both the blue and red GSE groups displayed a noticeable trend where metals are more heavily present than a specific iron abundance threshold, and we observed similar patterns in WUK. This indicates that the internal differences observed within GSE likely originated from uniform star formation processes across all three groups, and the difference between GSE and WUK might be attributed to variations in their respective star formation durations, with the blue and red GSE groups experiencing star formation over a shorter period of about 2 billion years, whereas WUK experienced it over a longer period of about 3 billion years. We propose that the difference between the blue and red GSE groups might be the result of metal production processes occurring after a specific point in time, rather than being caused by the internal differences observed within GSE itself.

Given an elementary finitely generated group $G$ and a connective spectrum $Z$ with sufficiently rapid growth in its truncations, a specific condition being met implies $Z$ being equivalent to the homotopy orbit spectrum of $Z$ over $Z[[G]]$. The result is applied to equivariant versions of $Z$ over an elementary finitely generated space $\sX$. The equivalent homotopy orbit spectra can be described as universal covers of certain monoid spaces consisting of invertible elements within equivariant powers of $Z$. This finding holds for non-connective form rings and is exemplified over the equivariant sphere spectrum for various forms including integral form rings of chains, alternating chains, and tense chains.

Acquiring labeled data is a costly process, thus reducing the cost per label without compromising accuracy is desirable. Selective labeling focuses on choosing the most informative samples for annotation, accelerating the convergence of learning algorithms. We introduce a label selection method based on the geometric properties of loss in regression, utilizing an efficient and fast algorithm to identify boundary samples, and then obtaining labels for them. This method is effective, efficiently executable, and works well even when labels are labels real-valued. Experimentation on diverse datasets shows it improves accuracy by 1-5% over other methods, and has a limited additional overhead of less than 2% compared to standard methods.

A comprehensive understanding of the electronic band structure at the interface of the spin gapless semiconducting heterostructure of EuS/InAs is achieved through a thorough investigation utilizing various techniques such as synchrotron radiation based photoemission spectroscopy, resonant photoemission spectroscopy, and first principles calculations. The findings of the experiments are then validated and interpreted by comparing experimental data with calculations, which in turn provide essential insights into the band alignment of the heterostructure and its internal structure, including the influence of surface states on the data. The synchrotron radiation based valence band measurements are found to be particularly informative in this context, which also highlights a significant contribution of dispersed states at the InAs valence band to the electronic structure at the interface.

We establish a direct connection between the Borel Wadge determinacy principle in second-order arithmetic and the combination of Borel Mendelsohn's $\Sigma^1_1$-Separation and Borel $\Pi^1_1$-admissibility. Additionally, our findings imply that Borel Wadge determinacy independently validates Borel $\Pi^1_1$-completeness.

Neural network models are often plagued by excessive computational costs, which can be mitigated by pruning unimportant connections. By prying open the internal connections of a network, rank-pruning methods directly operate on matrix elements, often resulting in significant performance degradation. To counter this issue, we introduce ClickTrain, a cutting-edge approach that integrates advanced optimization techniques with novel architecture search capabilities, enabling the creation of networks riddled with sparsity without compromising accuracy or efficiency. Unlike previous methods, ClickTrain focuses on adding high-value connections, facilitating the creation of networks with higher performance and greater accuracy. As a result, our technique achieves impressive outcomes, outperforming existing methods by up to 10% in terms of accuracy and allowing for a 95% reduction in memory usage, resulting in networks with 95% performance retention rates.

We define a substructural modal semantics framework based on ordered frames and demonstrate its effectiveness in establishing a sound and complete semantics for various substructural logic systems. Additionally, we show that this ordered frame approach is a useful tool for deriving structural completeness results for these logics.

The simultaneous observation of gravitational waves and electromagnetic radiation from neutron star mergers provides significant insights into coalescence events, with advances in technology driving the need for enhanced methods to process multi-messenger data. This work introduces an innovative technique that employs nested samplers to efficiently utilize various observables, contributing to a breakthrough in multi-messenger data analysis in real-time. The proposed method demonstrates its value through real-world neutron star merger cases, showcasing its potential to be adapted for applications where different data sources have varying levels of reliability.

TOI-5542b, a massive planet with ten times Earth's mass, orbits an extremely cool star just a few times hotter than the Sun's surface. As the first known planet around a star with such a low temperature, which is still relatively warm compared to the boundary where planets can no longer be directly detected, TOI-5542b offers a unique opportunity to examine the composition and formation of planets in a star with relatively mild conditions. Although the star's low temperature was a factor limiting the initial assessment of the planet's characteristics, the discovery of an accompanying outer companion, TOI-5542c, with more conventional conditions, indicates that the two planets are likely to be separated by a significant distance in a multi-planet system. With the expectation that further studies using space and ground facilities will yield more accurate information about the two planets' characteristics, the presence of these two planets in a low-temperature star environment may provide important insights into the formation of massive planets in relatively mild conditions.

We introduce a sampling-based algorithm that leverages primal-dual optimization techniques to effectively address and provide a theoretical framework for large-scale stochastic control problems involving distributional robustness. By utilizing an end-to-end learning approach, we show that naturally occurring learning algorithms converge towards primal-dual methods, which in turn allow for a significant improvement in operational policies at minimal cost. Experiments on two problems, one of which concerns flow network design and the other involves multi-agent systems under uncertainty, confirm the learning algorithm's efficacy and provide substantial enhancements to the existing policies.

Mathematical symbols are crucial for clear and effective communication in scientific and technical contexts. However, traditional mathematical notation often poses challenges for automatic recognition due to its limited coverage and complex format. A novel approach called MathSymNet is proposed to overcome these issues. MathSymNet consists of a convolutional neural network for extracting feature information and a kNN classifier to account for the diverse nature of mathematical symbols. By employing an end-to-end learning strategy, MathSymNet can be used for mathematical symbol recognition in real-time. Experimental results using datasets containing various types of mathematical symbols have demonstrated the efficacy of MathSymNet in achieving high accuracy and robust performance.

BPS states that arise from sheaves on ${{\bb{P}}^1}$ are well-documented, yet their counterparts on $({{\bb{C}}^2})^{K}/S_K$ introduce novel challenges, prompting an investigation into their growth patterns, which show remarkable exponential increase, with implications spanning across physics, especially within the fields of heptagon theory and conformal field theory.

In this study, we create a theoretical framework to analyze how epidemics spread in complex networks, and through this framework, we can calculate the probability that an initial infection will successfully spread throughout the entire network. This theoretical model is applied to various types of networks, and we demonstrate that by using key topological metrics such as bridgeness and coreness, we can accurately predict the spread of epidemics. Notably, we discover that networks with higher bridgeness or a more pronounced small-world structure tend to have lower probabilities of total outbreak occurrence. Additionally, we reveal a universal relationship between bridgeness and coreness that predicts outstanding outcomes in specific real-world networks, including the World Wide Web and co-authorship networks, regardless of whether initial infections are randomly distributed or concentrated in specific areas.

In the field of reinforcement learning, ensuring the safety of agents is a significant concern.  Current research employs various methods to account for safety restrictions by integrating them into the learning process, yet these approaches often result in prolonged convergence times.  To address this challenge, we introduce an innovative technique that leverages the Grouping of Similarity Constraints, allowing multiple safety restrictions to be fulfilled concurrently, thereby enabling faster reinforcement learning.  By clustering high-cost states associated with violating constraints and prioritizing clusters that represent the most severe risks, our method facilitates rapid adaptation and efficient compliance with a multitude of restrictions at once.  Experimental findings from clustering tasks and concurrent reinforcement learning demonstrate that our approach yields substantial improvements in performance and compliance with restrictions when dealing both independently and concurrently.

A new approach to identifying twin primes is presented, leveraging Lebesgue's concept of twin prime generators, L(n). Identifying a twin prime pair equates to locating a number 'a' that satisfies the equation a^2 - 1 = L(n). Two key formulas for calculating L(n) are provided, leading to novel formulas for the twin prime function, L(n+2) - L(n). One of these formulas, however, relies on an unsolved conjecture by Lebesgue. Additionally, one of the L(n) formula presentations bears resemblance to the Polignac formula, now L(n) = sum(a^(p-1)), which may offer an alternative approach to resolving the longstanding twin prime conjecture.

This paper presents a novel, two-tiered control system designed for mobile platforms equipped with sonar sensors to facilitate autonomous obstacle avoidance and safe navigation around the environment. The primary control layer ensures smooth movement of the mobile platform, whereas the secondary layer detects potential collisions and initiates corrective actions to avoid impacts. Each sonar sensor functions as an individual agent that tracks its respective axis on a predefined grid, with the control actions determined based on the gridded axes to optimize movement and minimize unnecessary actions. By implementing this autonomous system, effective collision avoidance and efficient task completion are achieved, which can be readily applied to various mobile platforms such as those used in automated farming and inspection of industrial facilities. Performance tests were conducted using both simulation and a physical platform, with results indicating successful implementation of the proposed control strategy.

The most distant known object in the solar system, Nereid, is particularly interesting due to its unusual properties, including its exceptionally low albedo. By utilizing high-resolution NIRSpec data from the James Webb Space Telescope, a detailed spectral analysis of this object was conducted. The analysis involved separating the spectrum into two components, accounting for both a continuum and water ice features. Comparing the spectral characteristics of this distant object to other large, icy objects revealed significant differences, suggesting that Nereid's surface is not primarily composed of water ice. Instead, the research suggests the presence of dark surface material, similar to that found in carbon-rich chondrites, which could be responsible for its unusually dark appearance.

We establish the conditions under which the affine planes, derived from the projective line over a specific type of numerical ring, can be expanded into fully-fledged projective planes. A crucial step involves creating the possible add-completion graphs for these circles and demonstrating that these add-completion graphs have a unique topology, thereby confirming their completeness. This approach also enables us to create new examples of finite projective planes, specifically those that are not isomorphic to existing ones, including two new examples with 91 points each.

We establish a method for demonstrating the implication from model A to model B in various contexts of cardinal characteristics by leveraging the Tukey-order. Specifically, this approach allows us to derive key equalities, such as $\text{b}=\text{d}=\text{f}$, without relying on countable support forcing techniques. For instance, this method provides a more intuitive understanding of Laver's equality $\text{b}=\text{d}$. Furthermore, we use this method to determine the possible relationships between $\text{b}$, $\text{d}$, $\mathfrak{p}$, $\text{s}$, $\text{a}$, and $\text{sa}$.

In a multi-arm bandit setup, we integrate the pessimism principle with Thompson sampling, resulting in a novel algorithm that boasts both probabilistic guarantees and improved efficiency. By leveraging the maximum likelihood estimator, our approach not only ensures accuracy but also enables time-complexity advantages, making it particularly suitable for the optimization of dynamic treatment policies and other large-scale learning problems. The theoretical analysis reveals that this algorithm achieves near-optimal regret bounds, a goal that was previously unattainable with algorithms based on Bayesian models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our algorithm has potential applications in specific tasks, such as multi-agent learning and online control, by providing both theoretical and empirical evidence of its effectiveness.

We establish invariance of certain subcategories consisting of finitely generated modules over completed group rings, which leads to the ability to transfer higher algebraic K-groups between groups with the same type of cohomology. This has significant implications as it provides concrete examples of modules with stable $SL$-invariance, illustrating the flexibility of the $SL$-invariance concept.

A common approach in studies of contextuality and nonlocality employs idealized models, typically represented by tables of probabilities, allowing conceptually similar ideas to be compared straightforwardly. This paper straightforwardly connects various quantum configurations, showing how they relate to one another and ultimately how they converge to each other, facilitating straightforward relations between the concepts of nonlocality, hierarchy, and contextuality.

In multi-band Hubbard models with degenerate orbitals, we focus on cases where the system's exact ground state exhibits exact pairing (eta-pairing), with the strongest pairing occurring at maximum orbital symmetry within a maximum orbital filling state. We developed a modified mean-field model that accurately captures the orbital behavior while preserving eta-pairing in the ground state, allowing for the calculation of critical interaction strengths for eta-pairing emergence based on the model. The results of this model align with those of a comprehensive numerical model-based study, which involved solving the system through an algorithm-based numerical model. The model-based approach also revealed that near the maximum orbital symmetry minimum, the critical coupling for the ground state's transition into a state with exact pairing decreases as the number of orbital symmetry bands decreases. The model-based approach offers a simple and insightful framework for analyzing the orbital behavior of multi-orbital Hubbard models with exact pairing ground states.

This work investigates p-adic solenoids and their applications in addressing certain functional equations. We find solutions to an equation analogous to the generalized Polya theorem, which involves the product of two a-adic solenoid characteristic functions. Furthermore, we investigate the limit of the normalized partial sums of the solutions as time approaches infinity. We also explore the connections between these findings and the infinite divisibility of the measures on p-adic integers derived from the solutions to the aforementioned functional equation.

Cluster analysis has been utilized for various scientific purposes, including ecological research, to identify patterns and groups within data.  However, when working with presence-absence data specifically, there are limited cluster analysis methods available due to the data format's incompatibility with traditional distance metrics.  As a result, researchers have turned to alternative methods such as Goldberger's use of second-order differences and Levenshtein distance.  Our study evaluates and compares four methods for clustering presence-absence data: the SOAL method, the Levenshtein distance, the Jaccard distance, and the Sørensen distance.  Through numerical experiments, we found that the performance of the SOAL method closely resembled that of the Levenshtein distance, outperforming the Jaccard distance and Sørensen distance which are commonly employed in ecological research.  Notably, we discovered that the computational cost of the SOAL method is relatively low, approximately half that of the Levenshtein distance, indicating its potential for use with large-scale data sets.

Salient object detection, a fundamental task in computer vision, focuses on pinpointing the most noticeable objects within an image. Recent advancements in this field have led to the development of various models, but they have been limited to processing specific types of images. We introduce a novel, integrated architecture that efficiently accommodates both standard and depth-based salient object detection tasks. By incorporating a depth-based approach, our model enhances its ability to accurately identify prominent objects even in complex environments. Additionally, we propose a novel attention mechanism, multi-channel attention, to optimize image processing and enhance detection accuracy. By merging this mechanism with the integrated structure, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on numerous benchmark datasets, surpassing existing methods while also demonstrating robustness across various visual representations.

This paper outlines ABUSI, a system designed for the ABUse System Challenge of SemEval 2019. Our ABUSI system excelled in identifying 80% of abusive content with high precision (43.1% accuracy) and effectively captured the required semantic meanings, resulting in a macro F1 score of 46.1%.

For a given base $b\geq 3$, integers that lack a palindromic representation when added to any of $1$, $b$, or $b^2$ in base $b$ are called nonrepresentable. It's been shown that nonrepresentable integers are less dense than those unrepresentable with the addition of just $1$ in base $b$. Furthermore, a related question has been answered by demonstrating that nonrepresentable integers when added to $1$, $b$, $b^2$, or $b^3$ in base $b$ have the same density.

We introduce a novel approach for CT image reconstruction that directly minimizes data misalignment, applicable to various types of measurements and noisy preprocessed data. By utilizing a conditional generative adversarial network, our method leverages a discriminator to account for various forms of noise in the generator's input and conditions its generative capabilities on an encoder's output, thereby producing images that accurately match the observed data and yielding high-quality reconstructions regardless of input distortions. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms conventional methods in simulating low-dose scans and in real-world applications under various degrees of noise, producing images with superior visual quality and more precise bone and lung edge detection.

This research paper presents a novel approach called Bayesian Program Learning (BPL), which utilizes the concept of implicit universal prior based on algorithm complexity to create a probabilistic framework for modeling programs with complex structures and patterns. BPL is particularly effective in high-dimensional settings, as demonstrated in our application of BPL to generate handwritten text from a minimal number of samples. BPL achieves this by implicitly encoding the probabilistic relationships between sequential components of programs, allowing for sample generation program-by-program, which can then be decomposed into a series of high-dimensional vectors. Our results show that BPL outperforms current handwriting models in terms of accuracy and generalization, achieving minimal character recognition errors even on unseen characters and words, and our code is available on our GitHub repository.

A new approach is proposed to create multi-nucleon matrix elements using an anisotropic basis within the Green's Function Monte Carlo method, allowing calculations of reactions involving up to six nucleons. By selecting specific basis anisotropies for each nucleon, we maximize the number of possible matrix elements. These are then calculated as individual components and combined to form the total interaction. As an alternative to the usual Green's Function Monte Carlo method's configuration expansion, a "basis-set transformation" technique is developed to prevent the matrix elements from becoming cumbersome. We show that this new method significantly reduces the storage needed and speeds up calculations involving complex six-nucleon states.

This study explores the application of quantum electronics principles in conjunction with advanced density-matrix methods to analyze multi-electron systems. By incorporating concepts of entanglement, researchers can differentiate between various current-carrying mechanisms in these systems and identify unique signatures of single- and multiple-electron transport. The findings demonstrate the capability of the used formalism to accurately model multiple-electron systems through detailed analysis of current-current correlator spectra, ultimately paving the way for the development of innovative devices such as entanglement detectors and single-electron memory units.

Let's consider a non-tangentially accessible domain $\Omega$ in complex 2D space that is bounded and convex. When it comes to the continuous pieces of complex-valued functions on this domain, we find that certain operators, denoted by $\Phi^*$, act on them in a way that corresponds to pulling back those functions after applying a function $\Phi$ from the disk and mapping it to $\Omega$. Given an important set of functions within those, called $BMOA$, it was proven that there's a way to characterize which functions from the disk, which end up producing a composition operator that maps the $BMOA$ functions within the disk to another set of $BMOA$ functions, depend on a specific type of mapping, which falls within the $BMOA$ set as well. Interestingly, the story changes when it comes to characterizing the set of complex functions that result from applying $\Phi^*$ which in turn produce $BMOA$ composition operators. In this context, we discover that a particular type of behavior, which relates to a different type of function, comes into play and influences the outcome.

All-order estimates of twist-four operator dimensions are provided for closed string theory, with anomalous dimensions corrected at two loops away from the AdS/CFT boundary. The exception is the lowest-dimensional twist-four operator, whose dimension correction is available at any order. The operator organization and the proposed method for determining anomalous dimensions are explained, with the approach validated by matching with available perturbative data.
